metadata.title: Critical Equations Inventory — Machine-Readable Complete Edition
metadata.description: Comprehensive machine-readable inventory of critical equations across all major academic disciplines. Each entry includes: canonical formula, description, role classification, domain of applicability, key assumptions (extracted from negation analysis), derivation summary, working numerical example, negation/failure case, source citation, and consensus status.

equations.name: Newton's Second Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: Newton's Second Law states that the net force acting on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration. It is the foundational equation of classical mechanics, connecting the cause of motion (force) to its kinematic effect (acceleration).
key_assumptions: (1) Velocity approaches the speed of light — a 1 kg object at v = 0.
equations.derivation_summary: Derivation from first principles: Newton postulated this as an axiom (Lex II) in the Principia. However, it can be derived from the conservation of momentum. Define momentum p = mv. For constant mass, dp/dt = m(dv/dt) = ma. Newton's Second Law then states F_net = dp/dt. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma. The law is consistent with Galilean relativity and can also be derived as the Euler–Lagrange equation for a free particle with Lagrangian L = ½mv² − V(x), yielding mä = −dV/dx = F.
equations.working_example: A 5 kg box is pushed with a net force of 20 N. Applying F = ma: a = F/m = 20 N / 5 kg = 4 m/s². Starting from rest, after 3 seconds the velocity is v = at = 4 × 3 = 12 m/s and the displacement is s = ½at² = ½(4)(9) = 18 m. This matches experimental observation for a frictionless surface.
equations.negation_failure_case: The equation breaks down when: (1) Velocity approaches the speed of light — a 1 kg object at v = 0.99c requires relativistic mechanics where F = γ³ma (the Lorentz factor γ ≈ 7.09 makes the effective inertia ~356 kg, not 1 kg). (2) At quantum scales — an electron in an atom does not follow a deterministic trajectory; the Schrödinger equation replaces F = ma. (3) For variable-mass systems (like a rocket), the naive F = ma gives wrong results; one must use the full F = dp/dt = m(dv/dt) + v(dm/dt).
equations.description: Newton's Second Law states that the net force acting on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration. It is the foundational equation of classical mechanics, connecting the cause of motion (force) to its kinematic effect (acceleration). It applies to all macroscopic, non-relativistic systems and underpins virtually every engineering calculation involving motion.

equations.name: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. This law explains planetary orbits, tides, and the trajectories of spacecraft.
key_assumptions: (1) Strong gravitational fields — near a black hole or neutron star, general relativity predicts effects (gravitational lensing, frame dragging) that Newton's law cannot account for.
equations.derivation_summary: Newton did not derive this law from more fundamental principles; he inferred it empirically. However, the inverse-square dependence can be derived by combining Kepler's Third Law (T² ∝ r³) with the formula for centripetal acceleration (a = v²/r = 4π²r/T²). Substituting Kepler's law: a = 4π²r/T² = 4π²r/(Cr³) = 4π²/(Cr²), showing a ∝ 1/r². By Newton's Second Law, F = ma ∝ m/r². By Newton's Third Law (symmetry in m and M), F ∝ Mm/r², giving F = GMm/r² where G is the proportionality constant measured by Cavendish (1798).
equations.working_example: Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and a 70 kg person on its surface (r = 6.371 × 10⁶ m). F = (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(70) / (6.371 × 10⁶)² = 686 N ≈ 687 N. This equals the person's weight mg = 70 × 9.81 = 687 N, confirming consistency.
equations.negation_failure_case: The law fails for: (1) Strong gravitational fields — near a black hole or neutron star, general relativity predicts effects (gravitational lensing, frame dragging) that Newton's law cannot account for. Mercury's perihelion precesses by 43 arcseconds/century more than Newtonian gravity predicts; only Einstein's field equations explain this. (2) Very large distances — galaxy rotation curves show stars orbiting faster than predicted by visible mass and Newton's law, leading to the hypothesis of dark matter or modified gravity (MOND).
equations.description: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. This law explains planetary orbits, tides, and the trajectories of spacecraft. It remained the definitive theory of gravity for over two centuries until superseded by general relativity for strong gravitational fields.

equations.name: Euler–Lagrange Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: The Euler–Lagrange equation provides the equations of motion for any mechanical system from a single scalar function, the Lagrangian L = T − V (kinetic minus potential energy). It is equivalent to Newton's laws but vastly more powerful for systems with constraints, generalized coordinates, and symmetries.
key_assumptions: or requires modification when: (1) Non-conservative forces are present (e.
equations.derivation_summary: Start with Hamilton's Principle: the actual path q(t) extremizes the action S = ∫ L(q, q̇, t) dt between fixed endpoints. Consider a variation q(t) → q(t) + εη(t) where η(t₁) = η(t₂) = 0. Then δS = ∫ [∂L/∂q · η + ∂L/∂q̇ · η̇] dt = 0. Integration by parts on the second term: ∫ (∂L/∂q̇)η̇ dt = [∂L/∂q̇ · η] (boundary terms vanish) − ∫ d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) · η dt. So δS = ∫ [∂L/∂q − d/dt(∂L/∂q̇)] η dt = 0. Since η is arbitrary, the integrand must vanish: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0.
equations.working_example: Simple pendulum of length l, mass m: Using angle θ as generalized coordinate, T = ½ml²θ̇², V = −mgl cosθ, so L = ½ml²θ̇² + mgl cosθ. Apply Euler–Lagrange: ∂L/∂θ̇ = ml²θ̇, d/dt(...) = ml²θ̈, ∂L/∂θ = −mgl sinθ. The equation gives ml²θ̈ + mgl sinθ = 0, or θ̈ + (g/l)sinθ = 0 — the standard pendulum equation. For l = 1 m, small angles: period T ≈ 2π√(l/g) = 2π√(1/9.81) ≈ 2.006 s.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Euler–Lagrange formulation fails or requires modification when: (1) Non-conservative forces are present (e.g., friction) — the standard Lagrangian cannot capture dissipation; one must add Rayleigh dissipation functions. (2) For systems with non-holonomic constraints (e.g., a rolling wheel that can slip), the standard variational principle does not apply directly and requires d'Alembert's principle or Lagrange multipliers. (3) At quantum scales, the classical action principle is replaced by the path integral formulation where all paths contribute.
equations.description: The Euler–Lagrange equation provides the equations of motion for any mechanical system from a single scalar function, the Lagrangian L = T − V (kinetic minus potential energy). It is equivalent to Newton's laws but vastly more powerful for systems with constraints, generalized coordinates, and symmetries. It is the foundation of analytical mechanics and extends to field theory, quantum mechanics, and general relativity.

equations.name: Hamilton's Equations
equations.domain_of_applicability: Hamilton's equations reformulate classical mechanics in phase space (position q, momentum p) using the Hamiltonian H (total energy for conservative systems). They reveal the symplectic structure of mechanics, provide the foundation for canonical transformations, and directly inspire quantum mechanical operator formalism.
key_assumptions: Non-relativistic regime
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Begin with the Lagrangian L(q, q̇, t). Define the canonical momentum p = ∂L/∂q̇. Perform a Legendre transformation: H(q, p, t) = pq̇ − L. Take the total differential: dH = q̇ dp + p dq̇ − ∂L/∂q dq − ∂L/∂q̇ dq̇ − ∂L/∂t dt. Since p = ∂L/∂q̇, the dq̇ terms cancel: dH = q̇ dp − ∂L/∂q dq − ∂L/∂t dt. From the Euler–Lagrange equation, ∂L/∂q = dp/dt. Comparing with dH = (∂H/∂q)dq + (∂H/∂p)dp + (∂H/∂t)dt, we get dq/dt = ∂H/∂p and dp/dt = −∂H/∂q.
equations.working_example: Harmonic oscillator: H = p²/(2m) + ½kx². Hamilton's equations: dx/dt = ∂H/∂p = p/m and dp/dt = −∂H/∂q = −kx. For m = 1 kg, k = 4 N/m, initial x₀ = 1 m, p₀ = 0: ω = √(k/m) = 2 rad/s. Solution: x(t) = cos(2t), p(t) = −2 sin(2t). At t = π/4: x = 0, p = −2 kg·m/s. Energy check: H = 4/2 + 0 = 2 J = 0 + ½(4)(1) = 2 J. Conserved.
equations.negation_failure_case: Hamilton's equations fail when: (1) The Legendre transformation is singular — if the Hessian det(∂²L/∂q̇_i∂q̇_j) = 0, one cannot solve for q̇ in terms of p (as occurs in some gauge theories). This leads to constrained Hamiltonian systems requiring Dirac's formalism. (2) For open/dissipative systems, H is not conserved and the symplectic structure is broken — one needs Caldirola–Kanai Hamiltonians or other extensions.
equations.description: Hamilton's equations reformulate classical mechanics in phase space (position q, momentum p) using the Hamiltonian H (total energy for conservative systems). They reveal the symplectic structure of mechanics, provide the foundation for canonical transformations, and directly inspire quantum mechanical operator formalism. The equations describe how a system evolves as a flow in phase space.

equations.name: Conservation of Energy
equations.domain_of_applicability: In any isolated system with conservative forces, the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) remains constant over time. This is one of the most fundamental principles in physics, extending beyond mechanics to thermodynamics, electrodynamics, and quantum mechanics.
key_assumptions: (1) Non-conservative forces act — a block sliding on a rough surface loses mechanical energy to friction (heat).
equations.derivation_summary: From Newton's Second Law: F = ma = m(dv/dt). Multiply both sides by v: F·v = mv(dv/dt) = d/dt(½mv²) = dT/dt. For a conservative force F = −∇V, F·v = −(dV/dx)(dx/dt) = −dV/dt. Therefore dT/dt = −dV/dt, giving d(T + V)/dt = 0, so E = T + V = constant. Alternatively, via Noether's theorem: if the Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence (∂L/∂t = 0), the Hamiltonian H = T + V is a conserved quantity.
equations.working_example: A 2 kg ball is dropped from height h = 10 m. At the top: T = 0, V = mgh = 2(9.81)(10) = 196.2 J, E = 196.2 J. At the bottom (h = 0): V = 0, so T = 196.2 J = ½mv², giving v = √(2×196.2/2) = √196.2 = 14.0 m/s. Verification: v = √(2gh) = √(2×9.81×10) = 14.0 m/s.
equations.negation_failure_case: Energy conservation fails when: (1) Non-conservative forces act — a block sliding on a rough surface loses mechanical energy to friction (heat). If a 1 kg block slides 5 m on a surface with μ = 0.3, it loses μmgd = 0.3(1)(9.81)(5) = 14.7 J to thermal energy. Mechanical energy is not conserved, though total energy (including heat) is. (2) In general relativity, global energy conservation does not hold in curved spacetime — there is no time-translation symmetry in expanding cosmological spacetimes.
equations.source_citation: Helmholtz, Über die Erhaltung der Kraft (1847)
equations.description: In any isolated system with conservative forces, the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) remains constant over time. This is one of the most fundamental principles in physics, extending beyond mechanics to thermodynamics, electrodynamics, and quantum mechanics. By Noether's theorem, energy conservation is a consequence of time-translation symmetry.

equations.name: Hooke's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The restoring force exerted by an ideal spring is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and directed opposite to that displacement. This linear force law is the simplest model of elasticity and governs small oscillations in virtually every physical system near a stable equilibrium.
key_assumptions: (1) Large deformations — stretching a real spring beyond its elastic limit causes permanent (plastic) deformation where F ≠ −kx.
equations.derivation_summary: Hooke's Law is empirical, but it can be derived as a first approximation by Taylor-expanding any potential energy function V(x) about a stable equilibrium at x = 0: V(x) = V(0) + V'(0)x + ½V''(0)x² + ... At equilibrium V'(0) = 0 and V(0) is a constant. So V(x) ≈ ½V''(0)x² = ½kx² where k = V''(0). The restoring force is F = −dV/dx = −kx. This shows Hooke's Law is universal for small displacements around any stable equilibrium.
equations.working_example: A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed by x = 0.15 m. The restoring force is F = −(200)(0.15) = −30 N (i.e., 30 N pushing back toward equilibrium). The potential energy stored is ½kx² = ½(200)(0.0225) = 2.25 J. If a 0.5 kg mass is attached, the oscillation frequency is f = (1/2π)√(k/m) = (1/2π)√(400) = 3.18 Hz.
equations.negation_failure_case: Hooke's Law breaks down for: (1) Large deformations — stretching a real spring beyond its elastic limit causes permanent (plastic) deformation where F ≠ −kx. A steel spring stretched beyond ~1% strain enters the nonlinear/plastic regime. (2) Materials like rubber exhibit hyperelastic behavior (Mooney–Rivlin model) where stress–strain is highly nonlinear. (3) At the atomic scale, interatomic potentials (e.g., Lennard–Jones or Morse potential) are strongly anharmonic for large displacements.
equations.description: The restoring force exerted by an ideal spring is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and directed opposite to that displacement. This linear force law is the simplest model of elasticity and governs small oscillations in virtually every physical system near a stable equilibrium. It forms the basis of simple harmonic motion.

equations.name: Centripetal Acceleration
equations.domain_of_applicability: An object moving in a circular path at constant speed experiences an acceleration directed radially inward (toward the center) with magnitude v²/r. This is a purely kinematic result from the geometry of circular motion and does not depend on the nature of the force providing the centripetal acceleration.
key_assumptions: (1) The speed is not constant — if the car is accelerating tangentially, there is an additional tangential acceleration component and the total acceleration is a = √(a_c² + a_t²), not simply v²/r.
equations.derivation_summary: Consider an object at position r(θ) = r(cosθ, sinθ) moving with constant angular velocity ω = dθ/dt. Velocity: v = dr/dt = rω(−sinθ, cosθ), with |v| = rω. Acceleration: a = dv/dt = −rω²(cosθ, sinθ) = −ω²r. This points radially inward with magnitude a = rω². Since v = rω, we get ω = v/r, so a = r(v/r)² = v²/r.
equations.working_example: A car travels around a curve of radius r = 50 m at v = 20 m/s. The centripetal acceleration is a = (20)²/50 = 400/50 = 8.0 m/s². For a 1500 kg car, the required centripetal force is F = ma = 1500 × 8 = 12,000 N, provided by tire friction. The minimum coefficient of friction needed is μ = F/(mg) = 12000/(1500×9.81) = 0.815.
equations.negation_failure_case: The formula fails when: (1) The speed is not constant — if the car is accelerating tangentially, there is an additional tangential acceleration component and the total acceleration is a = √(a_c² + a_t²), not simply v²/r. (2) The path is not circular — for an elliptical orbit, the radius of curvature varies and one must use the instantaneous radius of curvature, not the semi-major axis.
equations.description: An object moving in a circular path at constant speed experiences an acceleration directed radially inward (toward the center) with magnitude v²/r. This is a purely kinematic result from the geometry of circular motion and does not depend on the nature of the force providing the centripetal acceleration.

equations.name: Work–Energy Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy. This theorem is a direct consequence of Newton's Second Law and provides a scalar (energy-based) method for analyzing motion without needing to track vector forces and accelerations at every instant.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From F = ma along a path from position 1 to 2: W = ∫ F·ds = ∫ ma·ds = ∫ m(dv/dt)·(v dt) = ∫ mv·dv = ½m|v₂|² − ½m|v₁|² = ΔKE. The key step uses ds = v dt and the identity v·dv = d(½v²).
equations.working_example: A 1000 kg car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s. The net work done is W = ½(1000)(30²) − ½(1000)(10²) = 450,000 − 50,000 = 400,000 J = 400 kJ. If a constant force does this over 200 m, then F = W/d = 400,000/200 = 2000 N.
equations.negation_failure_case: Limitations: (1) For relativistic particles, the classical kinetic energy ½mv² must be replaced by (γ − 1)mc². A proton accelerated to 0.99c has KE = 5.7mc², not ½m(0.99c)² = 0.49mc² — the classical formula underestimates by a factor of ~11.6. (2) In thermodynamics, work on a gas (PdV work) changes internal energy, not just kinetic energy of bulk motion; the simple mechanical theorem doesn't capture microscopic degrees of freedom.
equations.source_citation: Coriolis, Du calcul de l'effet des machines (1829)
equations.description: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy. This theorem is a direct consequence of Newton's Second Law and provides a scalar (energy-based) method for analyzing motion without needing to track vector forces and accelerations at every instant.

equations.name: Impulse–Momentum Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: The impulse (force integrated over time) delivered to an object equals the change in its momentum. This is the time-integrated form of Newton's Second Law and is especially useful for collisions and impacts where forces are large but act over short durations.
key_assumptions: (1) Mass changes during the interaction (e.
equations.derivation_summary: From Newton's Second Law: F = dp/dt. Integrate both sides from t₁ to t₂: ∫ F dt = ∫ dp = p(t₂) − p(t₁) = Δp. The left side is defined as the impulse J. For constant force: J = F(t₂ − t₁) = FΔt = Δp.
equations.working_example: A 0.145 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s is hit by a bat, reversing its velocity to −50 m/s. The impulse is J = m(v₂ − v₁) = 0.145(−50 − 40) = 0.145(−90) = −13.05 N·s. If bat contact lasts Δt = 0.001 s, the average force is F = J/Δt = 13,050 N ≈ 13 kN (about 2930 lbs).
equations.negation_failure_case: The theorem in its simple form fails when: (1) Mass changes during the interaction (e.g., a bullet embedding in a block during a perfectly inelastic collision requires conservation of momentum for the system, not FΔt for one object). (2) In special relativity, p = γmv, so J = Δ(γmv) ≠ mΔv; the Lorentz factor must be included.
equations.description: The impulse (force integrated over time) delivered to an object equals the change in its momentum. This is the time-integrated form of Newton's Second Law and is especially useful for collisions and impacts where forces are large but act over short durations.

equations.name: Angular Momentum
equations.domain_of_applicability: The angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis equals its moment of inertia times its angular velocity. Angular momentum is conserved in the absence of external torques, explaining phenomena from figure skating spins to the stability of gyroscopes and the rotation of galaxies.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: For a rigid body, each mass element dm at distance r from the axis has velocity v = rω. Its angular momentum is dL = r × dm·v = r²ω dm. Integrating: L = ∫ r²ω dm = ω ∫ r² dm = Iω, where I = ∫ r² dm is the moment of inertia. Conservation follows from the rotational analog of Newton's Second Law: τ = dL/dt. If τ_net = 0, then L = Iω = constant.
equations.working_example: An ice skater with I₁ = 4.0 kg·m² spins at ω₁ = 2 rev/s. She pulls in her arms, reducing I to I₂ = 1.5 kg·m². By conservation: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂, so ω₂ = (4.0)(2)/(1.5) = 5.33 rev/s — she spins 2.67 times faster.
equations.negation_failure_case: L = Iω is insufficient when: (1) The body is not rigid — a deformable body (like a collapsing star) requires integration over changing mass distributions. (2) The rotation axis is not fixed or is not a principal axis — then L = Iω becomes the tensor equation L = I̲ω, where I̲ is the inertia tensor, and L and ω are generally not parallel (causing precession and nutation).
equations.description: The angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis equals its moment of inertia times its angular velocity. Angular momentum is conserved in the absence of external torques, explaining phenomena from figure skating spins to the stability of gyroscopes and the rotation of galaxies.

equations.name: Gauss's Law (Electric)
equations.domain_of_applicability: The total electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge. It is one of Maxwell's four equations and is the integral expression of Coulomb's inverse-square law.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Start with Coulomb's Law for a point charge Q at the origin: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) r̂. The flux through a sphere of radius R centered on Q is Φ = ∮ E·dA = [Q/(4πε₀R²)] × 4πR² = Q/ε₀. Since the flux depends only on the enclosed charge (not the surface shape), by the divergence theorem: ∮ E·dA = ∭ ∇·E dV = Q_enc/ε₀ for any closed surface. The differential form is ∇·E = ρ/ε₀.
equations.working_example: Find E outside a uniformly charged sphere (Q = 10 μC, r = 0.5 m). By symmetry, choose a spherical Gaussian surface at r = 0.5 m: E(4πr²) = Q/ε₀, so E = Q/(4πε₀r²) = (8.99×10⁹)(10×10⁻⁶)/(0.25) = 359,600 V/m ≈ 3.6 × 10⁵ V/m.
equations.negation_failure_case: Gauss's Law gives incomplete information when: (1) The charge distribution lacks sufficient symmetry — for an irregular charge distribution, the law is still true but E cannot be pulled out of the integral, making it useless for calculating E directly. (2) In materials with polarization, the bound charges modify the effective field; one must use D = ε₀E + P and ∇·D = ρ_free instead.
equations.description: The total electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge. It is one of Maxwell's four equations and is the integral expression of Coulomb's inverse-square law. It is particularly powerful for computing electric fields of highly symmetric charge distributions (spherical, cylindrical, planar).

equations.name: Gauss's Law (Magnetic)
equations.domain_of_applicability: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero, implying that magnetic monopoles do not exist. Every magnetic field line that enters a closed surface must also exit it.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Empirically, no isolated magnetic monopole has ever been observed. Theoretically, all known sources of B are either current loops or magnetic dipoles. For a magnetic dipole, B falls off as 1/r³ and the field lines form closed loops. For any closed surface around a dipole, every field line entering the surface exits elsewhere, so the net flux is zero. In differential form: ∇·B = 0, which follows from B = ∇ × A (the divergence of any curl is identically zero).
equations.working_example: Consider a bar magnet inside a closed box. Magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and loop around to enter the south pole. The flux through the top face of the box (where lines exit) is +Φ. The flux through the bottom (where lines enter) is −Φ. The total flux is +Φ − Φ = 0, confirming the law. If we numerically compute B for a dipole with moment m = 1 A·m² integrated over a sphere of radius 0.1 m, the net flux is exactly zero.
equations.negation_failure_case: If magnetic monopoles existed (as predicted by some grand unified theories and Dirac's 1931 quantization argument), then ∇·B = μ₀ρ_m ≠ 0, and Gauss's magnetic law would need modification. The flux through a closed surface containing a monopole of strength g would be Φ = μ₀g. Current experimental upper bounds from searches at the LHC and in cosmic rays constrain monopole abundance but have not found one.
equations.description: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero, implying that magnetic monopoles do not exist. Every magnetic field line that enters a closed surface must also exit it. This is one of Maxwell's four equations and reflects the fundamental difference between electric charges (which can be isolated) and magnetic poles (which always come in north–south pairs).

equations.name: Faraday's Law of Induction
equations.domain_of_applicability: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force (EMF) equal to the negative rate of change of that flux. This is the operating principle behind electric generators, transformers, and induction motors.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider a rectangular loop of width w moving with velocity v into a region of uniform magnetic field B. The flux is Φ = B × (area inside field) = Bwx where x = vt. The rate of change is dΦ/dt = Bwv. A free charge q in the moving conductor experiences force F = qv × B, doing work as it moves through the wire, creating an EMF = Bwv = dΦ/dt. The generalization to arbitrary loops and time-varying B fields gives ∮ E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt. In differential form: ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t.
equations.working_example: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.01 m² is in a magnetic field that decreases from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.02 s. EMF = −N × dΦ/dt = −100 × (0.01)(0.1 − 0.5)/0.02 = −100 × (−0.2) = +20 V. If the coil resistance is 5 Ω, the induced current is I = 20/5 = 4 A.
equations.negation_failure_case: Faraday's Law in its integral form can give misleading results when: (1) The 'circuit' is not well-defined — for a spinning Faraday disk (homopolar generator), the flux through the circuit appears not to change, yet an EMF is observed; the resolution requires careful treatment of the motional EMF (v × B) in the rotating frame. (2) In superconductors, the induced currents persist indefinitely and completely cancel any flux change, leading to the Meissner effect where dΦ/dt is forced to zero internally.
equations.description: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force (EMF) equal to the negative rate of change of that flux. This is the operating principle behind electric generators, transformers, and induction motors. The negative sign (Lenz's Law) ensures the induced current opposes the change in flux, consistent with energy conservation.

equations.name: Ampère–Maxwell Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop equals μ₀ times the sum of the enclosed conduction current and the displacement current (rate of change of electric flux). Maxwell's addition of the displacement current term was a critical theoretical insight that predicted electromagnetic waves.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Ampère's original law ∮ B·dl = μ₀I_enc fails for time-varying fields. Consider a charging capacitor: a current I flows in the wire, but no current crosses the gap between the plates. Taking an Ampèrian loop around the wire and two surfaces — one pierced by the wire (giving I), one passing between the plates (giving 0) — yields a contradiction. Maxwell resolved this by noting that between the plates, E is changing: ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀ d(EA)/dt = ε₀ A(dE/dt). Since E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A), we get ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = dQ/dt = I. Adding this displacement current restores consistency.
equations.working_example: A parallel-plate capacitor (plate area A = 0.1 m²) has a changing electric field dE/dt = 10⁶ V/(m·s). The displacement current is I_d = ε₀ A (dE/dt) = (8.85×10⁻¹²)(0.1)(10⁶) = 8.85 × 10⁻⁷ A ≈ 0.885 μA. The B field at radius r = 0.05 m from the axis is B = μ₀I_d r/(2πR²) (for r < R) or B = μ₀I_d/(2πr) (for r > R).
equations.negation_failure_case: Without Maxwell's displacement current term: (1) The equations would predict that electromagnetic waves cannot propagate — Ampère's original law with ∇ × B = μ₀J gives no wave solution. (2) Taking the divergence of Ampère's original law gives ∇·J = 0, which contradicts charge conservation (∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t) for time-varying charge distributions.
equations.description: The line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop equals μ₀ times the sum of the enclosed conduction current and the displacement current (rate of change of electric flux). Maxwell's addition of the displacement current term was a critical theoretical insight that predicted electromagnetic waves.

equations.name: Coulomb's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
key_assumptions: (1) Charges are in motion — moving charges produce magnetic fields and the full electromagnetic force is F = q(E + v×B) (Lorentz force), not just the electrostatic term.
equations.derivation_summary: Coulomb established this experimentally using a torsion balance. Theoretically, it can be derived from Gauss's Law: for a point charge q₁, the field is E = q₁/(4πε₀r²) r̂ (by symmetry). The force on a test charge q₂ is F = q₂E = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²) = kq₁q₂/r² where k = 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
equations.working_example: Two charges q₁ = +3 μC and q₂ = −2 μC separated by r = 0.1 m. F = (8.99×10⁹)(3×10⁻⁶)(2×10⁻⁶)/(0.01) = (8.99×10⁹)(6×10⁻¹²)/(10⁻²) = 5.394 N (attractive, since charges are opposite).
equations.negation_failure_case: Coulomb's Law fails when: (1) Charges are in motion — moving charges produce magnetic fields and the full electromagnetic force is F = q(E + v×B) (Lorentz force), not just the electrostatic term. Two parallel current-carrying wires experience magnetic forces absent from Coulomb's Law. (2) At quantum scales (distances ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m), quantum electrodynamics (QED) replaces the classical 1/r² law with virtual photon exchange, including vacuum polarization corrections that slightly modify the Coulomb potential at very short range.
equations.description: The electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. It is the electric analog of Newton's gravitational law and is equivalent to Gauss's Law for static fields.

equations.name: Lorentz Force Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The total electromagnetic force on a charged particle is the sum of the electric force (qE) and the magnetic force (qv×B). The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but does no work.
key_assumptions: Non-relativistic regime
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The electric force F_E = qE follows directly from the definition of the electric field. The magnetic force F_B = qv×B was established experimentally. It can be derived from special relativity: in the rest frame of a charge near a current-carrying wire, the Lorentz contraction of moving charges in the wire creates a net charge density, producing an electric force. Transforming back to the lab frame, this electric force appears as a velocity-dependent magnetic force qv×B. Einstein showed (1905) that magnetism is a relativistic effect of electricity.
equations.working_example: A proton (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at v = 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T (with E = 0). F = qvB = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(10⁶)(0.5) = 8×10⁻¹⁴ N. The radius of circular motion is r = mv/(qB) = (1.67×10⁻²⁷)(10⁶)/((1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(0.5)) = 0.0209 m ≈ 2.1 cm.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Lorentz force law is incomplete when: (1) Radiation reaction is significant — an accelerating charge radiates energy (Larmor formula), creating a self-force not included in qE + qv×B. The Abraham–Lorentz force adds a term proportional to the time derivative of acceleration. (2) In quantum electrodynamics, the classical continuous trajectory is replaced by quantum amplitudes, and the Lorentz force is replaced by the QED vertex interaction with virtual photons.
equations.description: The total electromagnetic force on a charged particle is the sum of the electric force (qE) and the magnetic force (qv×B). The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but does no work. This equation, combined with Maxwell's equations, provides a complete classical description of electromagnetic interactions.

equations.name: Ohm's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The voltage across a conductor is proportional to the current through it, with the proportionality constant being the resistance. This is the most widely used equation in electrical engineering, governing the behavior of resistive circuits.
key_assumptions: (1) Non-ohmic devices — a diode has I = I₀(e^(V/V_T) − 1), which is exponentially nonlinear.
equations.derivation_summary: Microscopically, Ohm's Law can be derived from the Drude model of electron transport. In a conductor, electrons experience an electric field E and collide with the lattice with average time between collisions τ. The drift velocity is v_d = eEτ/m_e. The current density is J = nev_d = (ne²τ/m_e)E = σE, where σ is the conductivity. For a wire of length L and area A: V = EL, I = JA, so V = (L/σA)I = RI, where R = L/(σA) = ρL/A.
equations.working_example: A 100 Ω resistor carries 0.5 A of current. The voltage drop is V = IR = (0.5)(100) = 50 V. The power dissipated is P = IV = V²/R = I²R = (0.25)(100) = 25 W.
equations.negation_failure_case: Ohm's Law fails for: (1) Non-ohmic devices — a diode has I = I₀(e^(V/V_T) − 1), which is exponentially nonlinear. At V = 0.3 V forward bias, I might be 10 mA; at V = 0.6 V, I could be 1 A — doubling V increases I by 100×, not 2×. (2) Superconductors have R = 0 below the critical temperature — current flows with zero voltage. (3) At very high current densities, resistive heating raises the temperature, changing R and making the V–I relationship nonlinear.
equations.description: The voltage across a conductor is proportional to the current through it, with the proportionality constant being the resistance. This is the most widely used equation in electrical engineering, governing the behavior of resistive circuits. It is empirical and applies to ohmic (linear) materials over a wide range of conditions.

equations.name: Biot–Savart Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The infinitesimal magnetic field contribution from a small current element Idl at a distance r. It is the magnetic analog of Coulomb's Law for computing B fields from arbitrary current distributions.
key_assumptions: (1) Currents are time-varying — the law assumes magnetostatics (steady currents).
equations.derivation_summary: The Biot–Savart Law is experimentally established from Oersted's discovery (1820) and Biot and Savart's measurements. It can be derived from Ampère's Law and the vector potential: B = ∇ × A, where A(r) = (μ₀/4π) ∫ J(r')/|r−r'| dV'. For a thin wire with J dV' = I dl', taking the curl gives dB = (μ₀/4π) I(dl' × r̂)/r². Consistency with Ampère's Law can be verified by integrating dB around a closed loop encircling the wire.
equations.working_example: Find B at the center of a circular loop of radius R = 0.1 m carrying I = 5 A. By symmetry, all dB contributions point along the axis. Integrating: B = μ₀I/(2R) = (4π×10⁻⁷)(5)/(0.2) = π×10⁻⁵ T ≈ 31.4 μT.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Biot–Savart Law fails when: (1) Currents are time-varying — the law assumes magnetostatics (steady currents). For rapidly changing currents, retardation effects become important and one must use the Jefimenko equations, which include the time delay r/c. (2) For current distributions that do not form closed loops (e.g., a finite wire segment), the Biot–Savart integral alone does not satisfy ∇·B = 0 unless the full circuit is included.
equations.description: The infinitesimal magnetic field contribution from a small current element Idl at a distance r. It is the magnetic analog of Coulomb's Law for computing B fields from arbitrary current distributions. Integration over the entire current path gives the total magnetic field at any point.

equations.name: Poynting Vector
equations.domain_of_applicability: The Poynting vector represents the directional energy flux (power per unit area) of an electromagnetic field. Its magnitude gives the rate of energy transfer, and its direction indicates the direction of energy propagation.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From Maxwell's equations, the energy density of the EM field is u = ½(ε₀E² + B²/μ₀). Taking du/dt and using Maxwell's equations: ∂u/∂t = ε₀E·(∂E/∂t) + (1/μ₀)B·(∂B/∂t). Substituting ∂B/∂t = −∇×E and ∂E/∂t = (1/μ₀ε₀)∇×B − J/ε₀, and using the identity ∇·(E×B) = B·(∇×E) − E·(∇×B), one obtains ∂u/∂t + ∇·S = −J·E (Poynting's theorem), where S = E×B/μ₀ is the energy flux.
equations.working_example: A plane EM wave in vacuum has E₀ = 100 V/m. Since B₀ = E₀/c = 3.33×10⁻⁷ T, the average Poynting vector is |S|_avg = E₀²/(2μ₀c) = (10⁴)/[2(4π×10⁻⁷)(3×10⁸)] = 13.3 W/m². This is the intensity of the wave. At 1 m from a 100 W light bulb (assuming uniform radiation): I = P/(4πr²) = 100/(4π) = 7.96 W/m².
equations.negation_failure_case: The Poynting vector gives paradoxical or misleading results in: (1) Static field configurations — a charged capacitor beside a permanent magnet has S = E×B/μ₀ ≠ 0, suggesting energy flow even though nothing is happening. The resolution is that the Poynting vector describes local energy flow, but the total flux through any closed surface is zero in this case. (2) In nonlinear or dispersive media, the simple S = E×B/μ₀ does not correctly represent the energy velocity; the group velocity must be used instead.
equations.description: The Poynting vector represents the directional energy flux (power per unit area) of an electromagnetic field. Its magnitude gives the rate of energy transfer, and its direction indicates the direction of energy propagation. It is essential for understanding electromagnetic wave energy transport, radiation pressure, and antenna power patterns.

equations.name: Ideal Gas Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The equation of state for an ideal gas, relating pressure, volume, number of moles, and temperature. It is a combination of Boyle's Law (PV = const at fixed T), Charles's Law (V/T = const at fixed P), and Avogadro's Law (V/n = const at fixed T, P).
key_assumptions: (1) High pressures/low temperatures where intermolecular forces matter — at P = 200 atm, CO₂ deviates ~30% from ideal behavior.
equations.derivation_summary: From the kinetic theory of gases: N molecules of mass m in a cubic box of side L. A molecule hitting a wall transfers momentum 2mv_x. The rate of wall collisions by one molecule is v_x/(2L). The total force on one wall is F = N(2mv_x)(v_x/(2L))/(L²) = Nm<v_x²>/V. By equipartition, ½m<v_x²> = ½k_BT, so P = F/A = Nk_BT/V. Since Nk_B = nR (where n = N/N_A and R = N_Ak_B), we get PV = nRT.
equations.working_example: 2 moles of gas at T = 300 K in a 0.05 m³ container. P = nRT/V = (2)(8.314)(300)/(0.05) = 4988.4/0.05 = 99,768 Pa ≈ 0.985 atm. This is close to atmospheric pressure, as expected for a reasonable-sized container.
equations.negation_failure_case: Fails for: (1) High pressures/low temperatures where intermolecular forces matter — at P = 200 atm, CO₂ deviates ~30% from ideal behavior. The van der Waals equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT corrects this. (2) Near the critical point or during phase transitions — at T_c = 304 K for CO₂, the gas liquefies and the ideal gas law is completely invalid. (3) Quantum gases (Bose–Einstein or Fermi gases at very low T) deviate fundamentally from classical ideal behavior.
equations.description: The equation of state for an ideal gas, relating pressure, volume, number of moles, and temperature. It is a combination of Boyle's Law (PV = const at fixed T), Charles's Law (V/T = const at fixed P), and Avogadro's Law (V/n = const at fixed T, P). It is the most widely used equation in gas-phase chemistry and thermodynamics.

equations.name: First Law of Thermodynamics
equations.domain_of_applicability: The change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system. It is the statement of energy conservation for thermodynamic processes, establishing that internal energy is a state function while heat and work are path-dependent transfer mechanisms.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The First Law is a generalization of the conservation of energy principle to include thermal energy. Historically, Joule's experiments (1843–1849) demonstrated the mechanical equivalent of heat: stirring water with paddles converts a measured amount of mechanical work W into a temperature rise equivalent to heat Q. Clausius formalized this: if only heat and work cross the system boundary, then by energy conservation, ΔU = Q − W. The internal energy U is proven to be a state function because the integral ∮ (dQ − dW) = 0 around any thermodynamic cycle.
equations.working_example: A gas in a piston absorbs Q = 500 J of heat and expands, doing W = 200 J of work on its surroundings. Then ΔU = 500 − 200 = 300 J. The gas's internal energy increased by 300 J, raising its temperature. For an ideal monatomic gas, ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, so ΔT = 300/((3/2)(1)(8.314)) = 24.1 K for 1 mole.
equations.negation_failure_case: The First Law does not fail, but can be misapplied: (1) If the system is open (mass crosses boundaries), the simple form must be extended to include enthalpy flux: dU/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ + Σ ṁ_i h_i. (2) In relativistic systems, internal energy includes rest mass energy (E = mc²), so nuclear reactions releasing binding energy require U to account for mass–energy conversion. (3) In cosmological contexts, the expansion of space does work on the vacuum energy in ways not captured by simple PdV work.
equations.description: The change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system. It is the statement of energy conservation for thermodynamic processes, establishing that internal energy is a state function while heat and work are path-dependent transfer mechanisms.

equations.name: Second Law of Thermodynamics (Entropy)
equations.domain_of_applicability: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. For any real (irreversible) process, the total entropy of the universe increases.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Clausius proved this by analyzing the Carnot cycle. For any reversible cycle: ∮ dQ_rev/T = 0, which defines entropy as a state function via dS = dQ_rev/T. For an irreversible process between states A and B: ΔS = S_B − S_A > ∫ dQ/T (the Clausius inequality). For an isolated system (Q = 0), this gives ΔS ≥ 0. The statistical interpretation (Boltzmann): S = k_B ln Ω. Since systems evolve toward macrostates with the largest number of microstates Ω, entropy increases.
equations.working_example: 1 kg of water at 80°C mixed with 1 kg at 20°C. Final temp: 50°C. Entropy change: ΔS_hot = mc ln(T_f/T_h) = (1)(4186)ln(323/353) = −371 J/K. ΔS_cold = (1)(4186)ln(323/293) = +412 J/K. Total ΔS = −371 + 412 = +41 J/K > 0. Entropy increases, confirming irreversibility.
equations.negation_failure_case: Apparent violations: (1) A refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot, apparently decreasing entropy of the cold reservoir. But the compressor does work, generating more entropy in the hot reservoir. Net ΔS_universe > 0. (2) Living organisms create local order (low entropy), but metabolic processes produce waste heat that increases environmental entropy by a larger amount. (3) Maxwell's Demon paradox: a demon sorting fast/slow molecules would violate the 2nd law, but Landauer showed (1961) that erasing the demon's memory generates at least k_BT ln 2 of entropy per bit.
equations.description: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. For any real (irreversible) process, the total entropy of the universe increases. This law establishes the arrow of time, defines the limits of heat engine efficiency, and explains why certain processes are spontaneous while their reverses are not.

equations.name: Boltzmann Entropy
equations.domain_of_applicability: Entropy is proportional to the natural logarithm of the number of accessible microstates consistent with a given macrostate. This is the bridge between microscopic statistical mechanics and macroscopic thermodynamics, explaining why entropy increases as systems evolve toward the most probable macrostates.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider two independent systems A and B in thermal contact. The total number of microstates is Ω_total = Ω_A × Ω_B (microstates are independent). Entropy must be additive: S_total = S_A + S_B. The only function satisfying f(Ω_A × Ω_B) = f(Ω_A) + f(Ω_B) is the logarithm. Therefore S = k_B ln Ω, where k_B is Boltzmann's constant determined by matching to the thermodynamic entropy of an ideal gas.
equations.working_example: A system of N = 100 coins, all starting heads-up (1 microstate: Ω_initial = 1, S_initial = 0). After shaking, the most probable state is 50 heads/50 tails with Ω_final = C(100,50) = 1.009 × 10²⁹. S_final = k_B ln(1.009 × 10² ) = (1.38×10⁻²³)(66.8) = 9.22 × 10⁻²² J/K. Entropy increased massively.
equations.negation_failure_case: Limitations: (1) For very small systems (N ~ 1–10 particles), fluctuations are large and entropy can spontaneously decrease over short timescales — this is described by the fluctuation theorem (Evans et al., 1993). (2) For systems with long-range interactions (gravity, unshielded Coulomb), the number of microstates may not be well-defined because the system lacks an equilibrium state — gravitational systems have negative heat capacity (they get hotter as they lose energy).
equations.description: Entropy is proportional to the natural logarithm of the number of accessible microstates consistent with a given macrostate. This is the bridge between microscopic statistical mechanics and macroscopic thermodynamics, explaining why entropy increases as systems evolve toward the most probable macrostates.

equations.name: Carnot Efficiency
equations.domain_of_applicability: The maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at temperature T_H and a cold reservoir at T_C. No real engine can exceed this efficiency, and only a perfectly reversible (Carnot) engine can achieve it.
key_assumptions: (1) One misidentifies the temperatures — using the boiler temperature instead of the actual steam temperature at the turbine inlet overestimates efficiency.
equations.derivation_summary: A Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. For the isothermal expansion at T_H: Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_2/V_1). For isothermal compression at T_C: Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_3/V_4). For the adiabatic steps: T_H V_2^(γ−1) = T_C V_3^(γ−1) and T_H V_1^(γ−1) = T_C V_4^(γ−1), which gives V_2/V_1 = V_3/V_4. Therefore Q_C/Q_H = T_C/T_H. Efficiency η = W/Q_H = (Q_H − Q_C)/Q_H = 1 − T_C/T_H.
equations.working_example: A power plant operates between T_H = 600 K (steam) and T_C = 300 K (cooling water). Maximum efficiency: η = 1 − 300/600 = 0.50 = 50%. If the plant absorbs Q_H = 1000 MW of thermal energy, maximum work output is W = 500 MW. Real plants achieve ~35–40% due to irreversibilities.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Carnot limit is violated if: (1) One misidentifies the temperatures — using the boiler temperature instead of the actual steam temperature at the turbine inlet overestimates efficiency. (2) If T_C = 0 K (absolute zero), the formula gives η = 100%, but the Third Law of Thermodynamics states absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps. (3) In practice, finite-time thermodynamics (Curzon–Ahlborn, 1975) shows that the efficiency at maximum power output is η_CA = 1 − √(T_C/T_H), which is significantly lower than Carnot.
equations.description: The maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at temperature T_H and a cold reservoir at T_C. No real engine can exceed this efficiency, and only a perfectly reversible (Carnot) engine can achieve it. It sets the fundamental thermodynamic limit on energy conversion.

equations.name: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The total energy radiated per unit surface area of a blackbody per unit time is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature. This governs stellar luminosities, thermal radiation from hot objects, and Earth's radiative energy balance.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Boltzmann derived this thermodynamically by treating radiation as a gas with pressure P = u/3 (where u is energy density) and using the First and Second Laws. Integrating Planck's Law B(ν,T) over all frequencies: j = ∫₀^∞ (2πhν³/c²)(1/(e^(hν/k_BT)−1)) dν. Substituting x = hν/(k_BT): j = (2πk_B⁴T⁴)/(c²h³) ∫₀^∞ x³/(e^x−1) dx. The integral equals π⁴/15, giving j = σT⁴ where σ = 2π⁵k_B⁴/(15c²h³) = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴).
equations.working_example: The Sun's surface temperature is T = 5778 K. Radiated power per unit area: j = (5.67×10⁻⁸)(5778)⁴ = (5.67×10⁻⁸)(1.115×10¹⁵) = 6.32 × 10⁷ W/m². Total luminosity: L = 4πR²j = 4π(6.96×10⁸)²(6.32×10⁷) = 3.85 × 10²⁶ W, matching observations.
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations occur when: (1) The object is not a perfect blackbody — real materials have emissivity ε < 1, so j = εσT⁴. Polished aluminum has ε ≈ 0.04, radiating only 4% of blackbody power. (2) At very low temperatures, quantum effects modify the radiation spectrum — objects cooled to nanokelvin temperatures radiate negligibly and the T⁴ law gives values below quantum noise floors.
equations.description: The total energy radiated per unit surface area of a blackbody per unit time is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature. This governs stellar luminosities, thermal radiation from hot objects, and Earth's radiative energy balance.

equations.name: Planck's Radiation Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: Describes the spectral radiance of electromagnetic radiation from a blackbody at thermal equilibrium as a function of frequency and temperature. It resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe of classical physics and marked the birth of quantum theory by introducing energy quantization E = hν.
key_assumptions: Non-relativistic regime
System at or near equilibrium
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Planck assumed that the energy of oscillators in the cavity wall is quantized: E_n = nhν (n = 0, 1, 2, ...). The average energy of an oscillator at temperature T is <E> = hν/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1) (from the Boltzmann distribution with discrete energies). The density of electromagnetic modes in the cavity is g(ν) = 8πν²/c³. The spectral energy density is u(ν) = g(ν)<E> = (8πhν³/c³)(1/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1)). The spectral radiance is B = cu/(4π) = (2hν³/c²)(1/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1)).
equations.working_example: Peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5778 K): Wien's Law λ_max = b/T = (2.898×10⁻³)/5778 = 501 nm (green light). At ν = c/λ_max = 5.99×10¹⁴ Hz: B = (2)(6.626×10⁻³⁴)(5.99×10¹⁴)³/(9×10¹⁶) × 1/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1) ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·sr·Hz).
equations.negation_failure_case: Classical prediction (Rayleigh–Jeans Law): B_RJ = 2ν²k_BT/c² ∝ ν², which diverges at high frequencies (ν → ∞) — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe.' Integrating over all frequencies gives infinite total energy. Planck's quantization cuts off the high-frequency modes because e^(hν/k_BT) ≫ 1 for hν ≫ k_BT, giving exponential suppression instead of the classical quadratic growth.
equations.description: Describes the spectral radiance of electromagnetic radiation from a blackbody at thermal equilibrium as a function of frequency and temperature. It resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe of classical physics and marked the birth of quantum theory by introducing energy quantization E = hν.

equations.name: Maxwell–Boltzmann Speed Distribution
equations.domain_of_applicability: The probability distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. It predicts that most molecules move near the most probable speed, with a long tail of high-speed molecules.
key_assumptions: System at or near equilibrium
Idealized conditions
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Maxwell assumed the velocity components v_x, v_y, v_z are independent and identically distributed. From the Boltzmann factor, the probability of a molecule having velocity v is proportional to e^(−mv²/2k_BT). In 3D, P(v_x,v_y,v_z) ∝ e^(−m(v_x²+v_y²+v_z²)/2k_BT). Converting to speed v = |v| with spherical coordinates introduces the factor 4πv² (the surface area of the speed shell). Normalizing gives f(v) = 4πn(m/2πk_BT)^(3/2) v² e^(−mv²/2k_BT).
equations.working_example: N₂ molecules (m = 28 u = 4.65×10⁻²⁶ kg) at T = 300 K. Most probable speed: v_p = √(2k_BT/m) = √(2×1.38×10⁻²³×300 / 4.65×10⁻²⁶) = √(178,065) = 422 m/s. Mean speed: <v> = v_p×√(4/π) = 476 m/s. RMS speed: v_rms = v_p×√(3/2) = 517 m/s.
equations.negation_failure_case: The distribution fails for: (1) Quantum gases at low temperature — bosons follow Bose–Einstein statistics (leading to BEC below T_c), and fermions follow Fermi–Dirac statistics (electrons in a metal have speeds near the Fermi velocity even at T = 0). (2) Non-equilibrium systems — a gas immediately after a shock wave has a bimodal or non-thermal speed distribution until collisions restore equilibrium. (3) Relativistic particles — the Maxwell–Jüttner distribution replaces e^(−mv²/2k_BT) with a relativistic energy term.
equations.description: The probability distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. It predicts that most molecules move near the most probable speed, with a long tail of high-speed molecules. It is fundamental to understanding gas properties, reaction rates, and effusion.

equations.name: Gibbs Free Energy
equations.domain_of_applicability: The Gibbs free energy is the thermodynamic potential that determines whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure. A reaction proceeds spontaneously if ΔG < 0.
key_assumptions: non-equilibrium thermodynamics where local temperature and pressure are not well-defined.
equations.derivation_summary: Start from the First Law: dU = TdS − PdV (for reversible processes). Define enthalpy H = U + PV, so dH = TdS + VdP. Define Gibbs energy G = H − TS, so dG = dH − TdS − SdT = VdP − SdT. At constant T and P: dG = 0 at equilibrium. For a spontaneous process at constant T, P: from the Second Law (dS_universe ≥ 0), one can show dG ≤ 0. The change in G equals the maximum non-PV work obtainable from the process.
equations.working_example: Water freezing at −10°C (263 K): ΔH_fus = −6.01 kJ/mol, ΔS_fus = −6.01×10³/273 = −22.0 J/(mol·K). At 263 K: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −6010 − (263)(−22.0) = −6010 + 5789 = −221 J/mol < 0. Freezing is spontaneous at −10°C.
equations.negation_failure_case: At +10°C (283 K): ΔG = −6010 − (283)(−22.0) = −6010 + 6227 = +217 J/mol > 0. Freezing is non-spontaneous at +10°C — ice melts instead. This demonstrates that the sign of ΔG depends critically on temperature and reverses at the equilibrium melting point (0°C where ΔG = 0). The equation breaks down in non-equilibrium thermodynamics where local temperature and pressure are not well-defined.
equations.description: The Gibbs free energy is the thermodynamic potential that determines whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure. A reaction proceeds spontaneously if ΔG < 0. At equilibrium, ΔG = 0. It combines enthalpic and entropic contributions to predict the direction of chemical and physical processes.

equations.name: Clausius–Clapeyron Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Relates the slope of a phase boundary in the P–T diagram to the latent heat of the transition and the volume change. It predicts how boiling/melting points change with pressure and is essential for understanding phase diagrams, weather systems, and industrial processes.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: At a phase boundary, the two phases are in equilibrium: G_1 = G_2. Moving along the boundary: dG_1 = dG_2. Using dG = VdP − SdT for each phase: V_1 dP − S_1 dT = V_2 dP − S_2 dT. Rearranging: (V_2 − V_1)dP = (S_2 − S_1)dT, so dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV. Since ΔS = ΔH/T at the transition, dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV).
equations.working_example: Boiling point of water at altitude: ΔH_vap = 40,700 J/mol, T = 373 K, ΔV ≈ V_gas = RT/P = (8.314)(373)/101325 = 0.0306 m³/mol. dP/dT = 40700/((373)(0.0306)) = 3567 Pa/K. At Denver (P = 83,000 Pa), the pressure drop is 18,325 Pa, so ΔT ≈ −18325/3567 = −5.1 K. Boiling point ≈ 95°C.
equations.negation_failure_case: The simplified form assumes ΔV ≈ V_gas = RT/P and that ΔH is constant. Near the critical point (T_c = 647 K for water), both assumptions fail: ΔV → 0 and ΔH → 0, so dP/dT becomes indeterminate (0/0). The phase boundary terminates at the critical point, and there is no longer a distinct liquid–gas transition.
equations.description: Relates the slope of a phase boundary in the P–T diagram to the latent heat of the transition and the volume change. It predicts how boiling/melting points change with pressure and is essential for understanding phase diagrams, weather systems, and industrial processes.

equations.name: Schrödinger Equation (Time-Dependent)
equations.domain_of_applicability: The fundamental equation governing the time evolution of quantum states. Given the initial wave function ψ(x,0), it determines ψ(x,t) at all future times.
key_assumptions: (1) Relativistic effects are important — for electrons in heavy atoms (Z > 50), speeds approach c and one must use the Dirac equation.
equations.derivation_summary: Schrödinger was guided by the de Broglie hypothesis (λ = h/p) and the classical wave equation. For a free particle with E = p²/2m and the plane wave ψ = e^(i(kx−ωt)), we need E = ħω and p = ħk. Time derivative: iħ∂ψ/∂t = Eψ. Space derivative: −ħ²∂²ψ/∂x² = p²ψ. Since E = p²/2m: iħ∂ψ/∂t = (−ħ²/2m)∂²ψ/∂x². Adding a potential V(x): iħ∂ψ/∂t = [−ħ²/(2m)∇² + V]ψ = Ĥψ.
equations.working_example: Particle in a 1D box (width L = 1 nm, electron mass). Energy levels: E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²). For n = 1: E_1 = π²(1.055×10⁻³⁴)²/(2×9.109×10⁻³¹×10⁻¹⁸) = 6.024×10⁻²⁰ J = 0.376 eV. For n = 2: E_2 = 4E_1 = 1.504 eV. The emitted photon wavelength for n=2→1: λ = hc/ΔE = 1100 nm (near-infrared).
equations.negation_failure_case: The Schrödinger equation fails when: (1) Relativistic effects are important — for electrons in heavy atoms (Z > 50), speeds approach c and one must use the Dirac equation. Gold's color (absorption at ~2.4 eV) is a relativistic effect absent from non-relativistic QM. (2) Particle creation/annihilation occurs — the Schrödinger equation conserves particle number, so it cannot describe pair production or radioactive decay. Quantum field theory is required.
equations.description: The fundamental equation governing the time evolution of quantum states. Given the initial wave function ψ(x,0), it determines ψ(x,t) at all future times. It plays the same role in quantum mechanics that Newton's Second Law plays in classical mechanics, but describes probability amplitudes rather than trajectories.

equations.name: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
equations.domain_of_applicability: It is impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle. This is not a limitation of measurement technology but a fundamental property of quantum mechanics arising from the wave nature of matter.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary:
For any quantum state ψ, define Δx = √( − ²) and Δp = √( −

²). Using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: |∫ f*g dx|² ≤ (∫|f|² dx)(∫|g|² dx), with f = (x̂ − )ψ and g = (p̂ −

)ψ. Since [x̂, p̂] = iħ, one derives (Δx)²(Δp)² ≥ |½<[x̂, p̂]>|² = ħ²/4. Therefore ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2. The minimum uncertainty is achieved by Gaussian wave packets.
equations.working_example: An electron confined to Δx = 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m (atomic size). Minimum momentum uncertainty: Δp = ħ/(2Δx) = (1.055×10⁻³⁴)/(2×10⁻¹⁰) = 5.27×10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s. Minimum kinetic energy: E = (Δp)²/(2m) = (5.27×10⁻²⁵)²/(2×9.109×10⁻³¹) = 1.52×10⁻¹⁸ J = 0.095 eV. This is the zero-point energy that prevents electron collapse into the nucleus.
equations.negation_failure_case: Common misunderstandings that fail: (1) Claiming that precise measurement of x 'disturbs' p (the 'observer effect' interpretation) — while historically used by Heisenberg, the principle is deeper: the particle simply does not have a definite position AND momentum simultaneously. (2) Attempting to violate the principle using entangled particles — EPR's 1935 argument suggested measuring x on particle 1 and p on particle 2 gives both. But the measured values are for different particles, and the correlations cannot be used to violate the principle for a single particle.
equations.description: It is impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle. This is not a limitation of measurement technology but a fundamental property of quantum mechanics arising from the wave nature of matter. It sets ultimate limits on the precision of all physical measurements.

equations.name: De Broglie Relation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Every particle has an associated wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. This wave–particle duality is the conceptual foundation of quantum mechanics, explaining electron diffraction, the structure of atoms, and the operation of electron microscopes.
key_assumptions: (1) Relativistic momentum is needed — for an electron at 0.
equations.derivation_summary: De Broglie reasoned by analogy with photons, for which E = hν and p = h/λ. He postulated that material particles also have wave properties with the same relation. This was confirmed by Davisson and Germer (1927), who observed electron diffraction from a nickel crystal with maxima at angles predicted by λ = h/p. The relation can be derived from the Schrödinger equation: a free-particle plane wave ψ = e^(ikx−iωt) has momentum eigenvalue p = ħk = h/λ.
equations.working_example: An electron accelerated through V = 100 V acquires KE = eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ J. Momentum: p = √(2mE) = √(2×9.109×10⁻³¹×1.6×10⁻¹⁷) = 5.40×10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. Wavelength: λ = h/p = (6.626×10⁻³⁴)/(5.40×10⁻²⁴) = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 1.23 Å — comparable to atomic spacings, enabling electron diffraction imaging.
equations.negation_failure_case: The simple formula fails when: (1) Relativistic momentum is needed — for an electron at 0.9c, γ = 2.29, so p = γmv = 2.29(9.109×10⁻³¹)(2.7×10⁸) = 5.63×10⁻²² kg·m/s, giving λ = 1.18×10⁻¹² m. Using p = mv (non-relativistic) would give λ = 2.69×10⁻¹² m, overestimating by 2.3×. (2) For massive macroscopic objects, the wavelength is immeasurably small — a 1 kg ball at 1 m/s has λ = 6.6×10⁻³⁴ m, far below any observable diffraction.
equations.description: Every particle has an associated wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. This wave–particle duality is the conceptual foundation of quantum mechanics, explaining electron diffraction, the structure of atoms, and the operation of electron microscopes.

equations.name: Born Rule
equations.domain_of_applicability: The probability density of finding a particle at position x is given by the squared modulus of its wave function. This statistical interpretation transforms the wave function from a physical wave into a probability amplitude, forming the interpretive foundation of quantum mechanics.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Born's Rule is a postulate of quantum mechanics rather than a derived result. However, Gleason's theorem (1957) shows that for Hilbert spaces of dimension ≥ 3, the only consistent probability assignment to measurement outcomes satisfying non-contextuality is P = |<ψ|φ>|², which reduces to |ψ(x)|² for position measurements. Additionally, Zurek (2005) showed the Born Rule can be derived from environment-assisted invariance (envariance) within decoherence theory.
equations.working_example: Hydrogen atom ground state: ψ(r) = (1/√π)(1/a₀)^(3/2) e^(−r/a₀) where a₀ = 0.529 Å. Probability of finding the electron within 1 Bohr radius: P(r < a₀) = ∫₀^a₀ |ψ|² 4πr² dr = 4/a₀³ ∫₀^a₀ r² e^(−2r/a₀) dr = 1 − 5e⁻² ≈ 0.323 (32.3%). The most probable radius is r = a₀ (where r²|ψ|² peaks).
equations.negation_failure_case: If one incorrectly uses |ψ| instead of |ψ|² (or uses the real part Re(ψ)), the probabilities would not be normalized and could even be negative. For a state ψ = (1/√2)(|+> + i|->), the correct probabilities are P(+) = |½|² = 0.5, P(−) = |i/√2|² = 0.5. Using Re(ψ) would give P(+) = 1/√2, P(−) = 0, which violates both normalization and experimental results.
equations.description: The probability density of finding a particle at position x is given by the squared modulus of its wave function. This statistical interpretation transforms the wave function from a physical wave into a probability amplitude, forming the interpretive foundation of quantum mechanics.

equations.name: Planck–Einstein Relation
equations.domain_of_applicability: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency. This was Planck's revolutionary hypothesis that energy is quantized in discrete packets (quanta), and Einstein extended it to explain the photoelectric effect.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Planck postulated this to resolve the ultraviolet catastrophe: cavity oscillators of frequency ν can only have energies E = nhν (n = 0,1,2,...). Einstein (1905) went further, proposing that light itself consists of quanta (photons) each carrying energy E = hν. Verification: photoelectric effect experiments show that the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons is K_max = hν − φ, with a sharp cutoff frequency ν_0 = φ/h below which no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity.
equations.working_example: Green light (λ = 530 nm, ν = c/λ = 5.66×10¹⁴ Hz): E = hν = (6.626×10⁻³⁴)(5.66×10¹⁴) = 3.75×10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.34 eV. A 1 W green laser emits N = P/E = 1/(3.75×10⁻¹⁹) = 2.67×10¹⁸ photons/second.
equations.negation_failure_case: Classical wave theory predicted that any frequency of light could eject electrons if the intensity was high enough (just wait for enough energy to accumulate). Experimentally, this is wrong: UV light (ν > ν_0) ejects electrons instantly even at low intensity, while intense red light (ν < ν_0) never does. Only E = hν with quantized photon energy explains the sharp frequency threshold.
equations.description: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency. This was Planck's revolutionary hypothesis that energy is quantized in discrete packets (quanta), and Einstein extended it to explain the photoelectric effect. It is the founding equation of quantum physics.

equations.name: Canonical Commutation Relation
equations.domain_of_applicability: The position and momentum operators do not commute — measuring position then momentum gives a different result than measuring momentum then position. This non-commutativity is the mathematical origin of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical mechanics.
key_assumptions: Non-relativistic regime
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: In the position representation, x̂ψ = xψ and p̂ψ = −iħ dψ/dx. Act with [x̂, p̂] on an arbitrary ψ: x̂(p̂ψ) = x(−iħ dψ/dx) = −iħx(dψ/dx). p̂(x̂ψ) = −iħ d(xψ)/dx = −iħ(ψ + x dψ/dx). Subtracting: [x̂, p̂]ψ = −iħx(dψ/dx) − (−iħ)(ψ + x dψ/dx) = iħψ. Since this holds for all ψ: [x̂, p̂] = iħ.
equations.working_example: For a Gaussian wave packet ψ(x) = (2πσ²)^(−1/4) e^(−x²/4σ²), compute <x̂ p̂> and <p̂ x̂>: <x̂ p̂> − <p̂ x̂> = iħ. For σ = 1 nm: Δx = σ = 10⁻⁹ m, Δp = ħ/(2σ) = 5.27×10⁻²⁶ kg·m/s. Product ΔxΔp = ħ/2, saturating the uncertainty bound (minimum uncertainty state).
equations.negation_failure_case: If we incorrectly assumed [x̂, p̂] = 0 (classical limit), then simultaneous eigenstates of x and p would exist, and the uncertainty principle would be violated. In path integral terms, this would mean all particle paths would have the same phase, and quantum interference — the basis of all quantum phenomena from tunneling to superconductivity — would vanish.
equations.description: The position and momentum operators do not commute — measuring position then momentum gives a different result than measuring momentum then position. This non-commutativity is the mathematical origin of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical mechanics.

equations.name: Mass–Energy Equivalence
equations.domain_of_applicability: Energy and mass are interconvertible. A body at rest possesses energy equal to its mass times the speed of light squared.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Einstein considered a body emitting two light pulses of energy E/2 in opposite directions. In its rest frame, its energy decreases by E. In a moving frame (velocity v), the Doppler effect changes each pulse's energy. Comparing total energy in both frames, the kinetic energy difference is ΔKE = E/(1 − v²/c²)^(1/2) − E ≈ Ev²/(2c²) for v ≪ c. Since ΔKE = ½Δm v², we get Δm = E/c², or E = mc².
equations.working_example: In U-235 fission, mass defect Δm = 0.186 u = 3.09×10⁻²  kg per nucleus. E = Δmc² = (3.09×10⁻² )(9×10¹⁶) = 2.78×10⁻¹¹ J = 174 MeV. 1 kg of U-235 (2.56×10²⁴ atoms): total E = 7.1×10¹³ J ≈ equivalent to 1700 tons of TNT.
equations.negation_failure_case: If mass–energy equivalence did not hold, nuclear binding energies would not account for the observed mass of nuclei. The helium-4 nucleus would weigh 4.032 u (sum of parts) instead of the observed 4.0026 u. The 'missing' 0.030 u = 28 MeV of binding energy would have no explanation. Similarly, positron–electron annihilation producing 1.022 MeV of gamma rays would violate energy conservation without E = mc².
equations.description: Energy and mass are interconvertible. A body at rest possesses energy equal to its mass times the speed of light squared. This explains the enormous energy released in nuclear reactions and is the basis for nuclear power and weapons.

equations.name: Lorentz Factor
equations.domain_of_applicability: The Lorentz factor quantifies the magnitude of time dilation, length contraction, and relativistic mass increase. At v = 0 it equals 1 (no relativistic effects); it diverges as v approaches c, making the speed of light an absolute speed limit for massive objects.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Derived from Einstein's two postulates: (1) laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, (2) the speed of light is constant. Consider a light clock (light bouncing between mirrors separated by distance d). In its rest frame, the tick time is Δt₀ = 2d/c. In a frame where the clock moves at velocity v, the light path is longer: 2√(d² + (vΔt/2)²) = cΔt. Solving: Δt = 2d/(c√(1−v²/c²)) = γΔt₀.
equations.working_example: Muons produced in the upper atmosphere at v = 0.998c: γ = 1/√(1−0.996) = 1/√(0.004) = 15.8. Rest-frame half-life is 1.56 μs. In Earth's frame: τ = γτ₀ = 15.8 × 1.56 = 24.6 μs. In 24.6 μs at 0.998c, muons travel d = 0.998×3×10⁸×24.6×10⁻⁶ = 7.37 km — enough to reach the ground, as observed.
equations.negation_failure_case: Without γ, muons with τ = 1.56 μs would travel only 0.998c × 1.56×10⁻⁶ = 467 m before half decay. From a production altitude of ~15 km, virtually none would reach the ground. Yet detectors observe significant muon flux at sea level — a direct confirmation of time dilation.
equations.description: The Lorentz factor quantifies the magnitude of time dilation, length contraction, and relativistic mass increase. At v = 0 it equals 1 (no relativistic effects); it diverges as v approaches c, making the speed of light an absolute speed limit for massive objects.

equations.name: Einstein Field Equations
equations.domain_of_applicability: The fundamental equations of general relativity, relating the curvature of spacetime (left side) to the distribution of mass and energy (right side). They predict gravitational waves, black holes, the expansion of the universe, and gravitational lensing.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Einstein required: (1) equations reduce to Newton's gravity in the weak-field limit, (2) covariant under general coordinate transformations, (3) involve second derivatives of the metric g_μν. The most general second-order tensor satisfying the Bianchi identity ∇_μ G^μν = 0 is G_μν = R_μν − ½Rg_μν (the Einstein tensor, built from the Riemann curvature). Energy conservation ∇_μ T^μν = 0 matches. The coupling constant 8πG/c⁴ is fixed by the Newtonian limit.
equations.working_example: Schwarzschild solution (spherically symmetric vacuum T_μν = 0): ds² = −(1−2GM/(rc²))c²dt² + dr²/(1−2GM/(rc²)) + r²dΩ². For the Sun: r_s = 2GM/c² = 2.95 km. Light bending angle: α = 4GM/(rc²) = 1.75 arcseconds at the solar limb, confirmed by Eddington (1919).
equations.negation_failure_case: At quantum scales (Planck length l_P = 1.6×10⁻³⁵ m), the field equations predict singularities (infinite curvature) inside black holes and at the Big Bang. These singularities signal the breakdown of GR. A quantum theory of gravity (string theory, loop quantum gravity) is needed but remains unfinished. Additionally, the cosmological constant Λ predicted by quantum field theory exceeds the observed value by ~120 orders of magnitude (the cosmological constant problem).
equations.description: The fundamental equations of general relativity, relating the curvature of spacetime (left side) to the distribution of mass and energy (right side). They predict gravitational waves, black holes, the expansion of the universe, and gravitational lensing.

equations.name: Friedmann Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Governs the expansion rate of the universe. Derived from Einstein's field equations assuming a homogeneous, isotropic universe (the cosmological principle).
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Start with the FRW metric: ds² = −c²dt² + a(t)²[dr²/(1−kr²) + r²dΩ²] and T_μν for a perfect fluid. The 00-component of Einstein's equations gives (ȧ/a)² = 8πGρ/3 − kc²/a² + Λc²/3. This can also be derived by Newtonian analogy: consider a shell of mass m at the edge of an expanding sphere, apply energy conservation E = ½mv² − GMm/r, and use v = Hr, M = (4/3)πr³ρ.
equations.working_example: Current universe: H₀ = 67.4 km/s/Mpc = 2.18×10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Critical density: ρ_c = 3H₀²/(8πG) = 8.53×10⁻²⁷ kg/m³. Observations: Ω_m = 0.315 (matter), Ω_Λ = 0.685 (dark energy), Ω_k ≈ 0 (flat). Age of universe: t₀ ≈ 1/H₀ × (correction factor) ≈ 13.8 Gyr.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Friedmann equation assumes perfect homogeneity. In the real universe, inhomogeneities (voids, clusters) cause backreaction effects that may mimic dark energy at the ~1–5% level (Buchert et al., Gen. Relativ. Gravit., 2012). If Λ is set to zero and inhomogeneities are ignored, the predicted age of the universe (~9 Gyr for matter-dominated) contradicts the observed ages of the oldest stars (~12+ Gyr).
equations.description: Governs the expansion rate of the universe. Derived from Einstein's field equations assuming a homogeneous, isotropic universe (the cosmological principle). It relates the Hubble parameter H = ȧ/a to the energy density, spatial curvature, and cosmological constant.

equations.name: Hubble's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The recessional velocity of distant galaxies is proportional to their distance, with Hubble's constant as the proportionality factor. This was the observational discovery of the expanding universe and remains the foundation of observational cosmology.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric, the proper distance to a comoving galaxy is d(t) = a(t)r. Its velocity is v = ḋ = ȧ r = (ȧ/a)(ar) = Hd, where H = ȧ/a is the Hubble parameter. Hubble measured redshifts z = Δλ/λ of galaxies and their distances (via Cepheid variables), finding a linear relation v = cz ≈ H₀d for z ≪ 1.
equations.working_example: A galaxy at d = 100 Mpc: v = H₀d = (70 km/s/Mpc)(100 Mpc) = 7,000 km/s. Its redshift: z = v/c = 7000/300000 = 0.023. Observed spectrum of hydrogen Lyman-α (λ₀ = 121.6 nm) shifts to λ = 121.6(1+0.023) = 124.4 nm.
equations.negation_failure_case: Hubble's Law (v = H₀d) is only valid for 'nearby' galaxies (z < ~0.1). At cosmological distances, the linear relation breaks down. A galaxy at z = 2 has v_recession > c (superluminal), which is allowed in GR (space itself expands). Using v = H₀d would give d = v/H₀ = cz/H₀ = 8,571 Mpc, but the correct comoving distance is ~5,200 Mpc. The linear approximation overestimates by 65%.
equations.description: The recessional velocity of distant galaxies is proportional to their distance, with Hubble's constant as the proportionality factor. This was the observational discovery of the expanding universe and remains the foundation of observational cosmology.

equations.name: Navier–Stokes Equations
equations.domain_of_applicability: The fundamental equations governing viscous fluid flow, expressing Newton's Second Law for a continuum. They describe everything from blood flow to weather patterns to aircraft aerodynamics.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Apply Newton's Second Law to a fluid element of volume dV: ρ dV (Dv/Dt) = sum of forces. Pressure force: −∇P dV. Viscous force: for a Newtonian fluid, stress tensor τ_ij = μ(∂v_i/∂x_j + ∂v_j/∂x_i), giving a net force μ∇²v dV (for incompressible flow). Gravity: ρg dV. Dividing by ρ dV: Dv/Dt = −∇P/ρ + ν∇²v + g, where ν = μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity.
equations.working_example: Laminar flow in a pipe (Hagen–Poiseuille): for water (μ = 10⁻³ Pa·s) in a pipe of radius R = 0.01 m, length L = 1 m, with ΔP = 100 Pa: Q = πR⁴ΔP/(8μL) = π(10⁻⁸)(100)/(8×10⁻³) = 3.93×10⁻⁴ m³/s = 0.393 L/s. Max velocity (at center): v_max = 2Q/(πR²) = 2.50 m/s.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Navier–Stokes equations become computationally intractable for turbulent flow (Re > ~4000).
