Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulence at Re = 10⁶ would require ~10¹⁸ grid points — beyond any foreseeable computer. Engineers use Reynolds-averaged (RANS) or Large Eddy Simulation (LES) approximations, which introduce empirical turbulence models that can fail for separated flows, rotating systems, or strong pressure gradients.
equations.description: The fundamental equations governing viscous fluid flow, expressing Newton's Second Law for a continuum. They describe everything from blood flow to weather patterns to aircraft aerodynamics. Proving whether smooth solutions always exist in 3D is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems.

equations.name: Bernoulli's Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Along a streamline in steady, inviscid, incompressible flow, the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure, and hydrostatic pressure is constant. It explains airplane lift, venturi meters, and why a curveball curves.
key_assumptions: (1) Viscosity matters — in long pipes, frictional losses cause pressure drops not accounted for.
equations.derivation_summary: Apply the work–energy theorem to a fluid parcel moving along a streamline. Work by pressure forces: dW_P = P₁A₁ds₁ − P₂A₂ds₂. By continuity, A₁ds₁ = A₂ds₂ = dV. Work by gravity: dW_g = −ρg dV (h₂ − h₁). Change in KE: dKE = ½ρ dV(v₂² − v₁²). Setting dW = dKE: P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂.
equations.working_example: A venturi meter: pipe diameter narrows from 10 cm to 5 cm. Upstream v₁ = 2 m/s. By continuity: v₂ = v₁(A₁/A₂) = 2(10²/5²) = 8 m/s. Pressure drop (horizontal): ΔP = ½ρ(v₂²−v₁²) = ½(1000)(64−4) = 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa.
equations.negation_failure_case: Bernoulli's equation fails when: (1) Viscosity matters — in long pipes, frictional losses cause pressure drops not accounted for. Adding a head loss term: P₁/ρg + v₁²/2g + h₁ = P₂/ρg + v₂²/2g + h₂ + h_f. (2) The flow is unsteady (time-dependent), requiring the unsteady Bernoulli equation. (3) The flow is compressible (Ma > 0.3), requiring compressible flow relations.
equations.description: Along a streamline in steady, inviscid, incompressible flow, the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure, and hydrostatic pressure is constant. It explains airplane lift, venturi meters, and why a curveball curves.

equations.name: Reynolds Number
equations.domain_of_applicability: A dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces that predicts the flow regime: laminar (Re < ~2300 for pipes), transitional, or turbulent (Re > ~4000). It is the most important parameter in fluid dynamics for scaling and similarity analysis.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Non-dimensionalize the Navier–Stokes equations using characteristic scales: length L, velocity U, time L/U, pressure ρU². The momentum equation becomes: Dv*/Dt* = −∇*P* + (1/Re)∇*²v* + (1/Fr²)g*, where Re = ρUL/μ appears naturally as the coefficient of the viscous term. When Re ≫ 1, viscous forces are negligible compared to inertial forces (turbulent regime); when Re ≪ 1, viscosity dominates (creeping/Stokes flow).
equations.working_example: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 10⁻³ Pa·s) flowing at v = 1 m/s through a pipe of diameter D = 0.05 m: Re = (1000)(1)(0.05)/(10⁻³) = 50,000. This is well into the turbulent regime (> 4000). For honey (μ ≈ 5 Pa·s) at the same conditions: Re = (1400)(1)(0.05)/5 = 14 — deep in the laminar regime.
equations.negation_failure_case: Reynolds number alone is insufficient for: (1) Non-Newtonian fluids (blood, polymers) where μ depends on shear rate — a shear-thinning fluid may be turbulent at one shear rate and laminar at another. (2) Rotating flows, where the Taylor number replaces Re. (3) Flows with significant buoyancy, where the Rayleigh number governs the transition to convective turbulence.
equations.description: A dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces that predicts the flow regime: laminar (Re < ~2300 for pipes), transitional, or turbulent (Re > ~4000). It is the most important parameter in fluid dynamics for scaling and similarity analysis.

equations.name: Poiseuille's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The volumetric flow rate through a long, straight, cylindrical tube under laminar conditions. The r⁴ dependence means that halving a vessel's radius reduces flow by a factor of 16, which is critical in understanding blood flow and vascular resistance.
key_assumptions: (1) Re > ~2300 and the flow becomes turbulent — turbulent flow has much higher resistance.
equations.derivation_summary: Solve the Navier–Stokes equations for steady, fully developed, axisymmetric flow in a pipe. In cylindrical coordinates: 0 = −dP/dz + μ(1/r)d/dr(r dv_z/dr). Integrating twice with boundary conditions v_z(R) = 0 and v_z finite at r = 0: v_z(r) = (ΔP/4μL)(R² − r²). Flow rate: Q = ∫₀^R v_z(r) 2πr dr = πΔPR⁴/(8μL).
equations.working_example: Blood flow in an arteriole: r = 0.5 mm = 5×10⁻⁴ m, L = 0.01 m, ΔP = 4000 Pa, μ = 3.5×10⁻³ Pa·s. Q = π(5×10⁻⁴)⁴(4000)/(8×3.5×10⁻³×0.01) = π(6.25×10⁻¹⁴)(4000)/(2.8×10⁻⁴) = 2.8×10⁻⁶ m³/s. If the radius decreases 50% (atherosclerosis): Q_new = Q/16 = 1.75×10⁻⁷ m³/s — a 94% reduction in flow.
equations.negation_failure_case: Poiseuille's law fails when: (1) Re > ~2300 and the flow becomes turbulent — turbulent flow has much higher resistance. (2) The tube is short (entrance effects mean the flow is not fully developed). (3) The fluid is non-Newtonian (blood is shear-thinning, so μ varies with shear rate, and the velocity profile is blunted compared to the parabolic Poiseuille profile).
equations.description: The volumetric flow rate through a long, straight, cylindrical tube under laminar conditions. The r⁴ dependence means that halving a vessel's radius reduces flow by a factor of 16, which is critical in understanding blood flow and vascular resistance.

equations.name: Stokes' Drag Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The drag force on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid at low Reynolds number. It governs sedimentation of particles, aerosol physics, and the motion of microorganisms in water.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Solve the Stokes equations (Navier–Stokes with Re ≪ 1, neglecting the inertial term): 0 = −∇P + μ∇²v, ∇·v = 0, with boundary conditions v = U at r → ∞ and v = 0 on the sphere surface. The solution gives the velocity and pressure fields, from which the stress tensor is computed. Integrating the stress over the sphere surface yields: F_d = 6πμRU (2/3 from pressure drag, 1/3 from viscous shear).
equations.working_example: A 10 μm diameter water droplet falling through air (μ = 1.8×10⁻⁵ Pa·s). Terminal velocity: mg = 6πμrv, so v = (2r²Δρ g)/(9μ) = (2×(5×10⁻⁶)²×1000×9.81)/(9×1.8×10⁻⁵) = 3.0×10⁻³ m/s = 3 mm/s. Re = ρ_air v(2r)/μ = (1.2)(0.003)(10⁻⁵)/(1.8×10⁻⁵) = 0.002 ≪ 1, confirming Stokes regime.
equations.negation_failure_case: At higher Re (Re > ~1), the Stokes formula underestimates drag. For a baseball (r = 0.037 m, v = 40 m/s, Re ≈ 10⁵): F_Stokes = 6π(1.8×10⁻⁵)(0.037)(40) = 5.0×10⁻⁴ N. Actual drag: F = ½C_dρAv² = ½(0.4)(1.2)(π×0.037²)(1600) = 1.65 N — over 3000× larger. The Stokes formula is completely inapplicable at high Re.
equations.description: The drag force on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid at low Reynolds number. It governs sedimentation of particles, aerosol physics, and the motion of microorganisms in water.

equations.name: Snell's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: Relates the angles of incidence and refraction when light passes between two media with different refractive indices. It governs lens design, fiber optics, and the apparent bending of objects underwater.
key_assumptions: or requires modification for: (1) Total internal reflection — when n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁), sinθ₂ > 1, which has no real solution.
equations.derivation_summary: From Fermat's principle of least time: light takes the path that minimizes travel time between two points. If point A is in medium 1 and point B in medium 2 (with speeds v₁ = c/n₁ and v₂ = c/n₂), the total time is T = √(x²+a²)/(c/n₁) + √((d−x)²+b²)/(c/n₂). Minimizing dT/dx = 0: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂. Alternatively, it follows from the boundary condition that the tangential component of the wave vector is continuous across the interface.
equations.working_example: Light passing from air (n₁ = 1.00) into water (n₂ = 1.33) at θ₁ = 45°: sinθ₂ = (n₁/n₂)sinθ₁ = (1/1.33)(0.707) = 0.531, so θ₂ = 32.1°. The light bends toward the normal upon entering the denser medium.
equations.negation_failure_case: Snell's Law fails or requires modification for: (1) Total internal reflection — when n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁), sinθ₂ > 1, which has no real solution. The light is totally reflected. For water→air: θ_c = arcsin(1/1.33) = 48.8°. (2) Metamaterials with negative refractive index n < 0 cause the refracted ray to bend on the same side of the normal (Veselago, 1968).
equations.description: Relates the angles of incidence and refraction when light passes between two media with different refractive indices. It governs lens design, fiber optics, and the apparent bending of objects underwater.

equations.name: Photoelectric Effect
equations.domain_of_applicability: The maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected from a metal surface by light equals the photon energy minus the work function. Einstein's explanation earned him the Nobel Prize and provided definitive evidence for energy quantization.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Einstein postulated that light consists of photons, each with energy E = hν. When a photon is absorbed by a surface electron, the electron gains energy hν. To escape the metal, it must overcome the work function φ (minimum binding energy). The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron (one that was at the surface and needed only φ to escape) is K_max = hν − φ. If hν < φ, no electrons are emitted regardless of light intensity.
equations.working_example: UV light (λ = 250 nm, ν = 1.2×10¹⁵ Hz) on sodium (φ = 2.28 eV): K_max = hν − φ = (6.626×10⁻³⁴)(1.2×10¹⁵)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) − 2.28 = 4.97 − 2.28 = 2.69 eV. Stopping voltage: V_s = K_max/e = 2.69 V.
equations.negation_failure_case: Classical wave theory predicts: (1) K_max should increase with light intensity — wrong; only the number of electrons increases with intensity. (2) Any frequency should work if you wait long enough — wrong; below threshold frequency ν₀ = φ/h, no electrons are emitted even at extreme intensities. (3) There should be a time delay for energy accumulation — wrong; emission is instantaneous (< 10⁻⁹ s). All three classical predictions are violated.
equations.description: The maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected from a metal surface by light equals the photon energy minus the work function. Einstein's explanation earned him the Nobel Prize and provided definitive evidence for energy quantization.

equations.name: Radioactive Decay Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The number of undecayed radioactive nuclei decreases exponentially over time. Each nucleus has a constant probability λ of decaying per unit time, independent of its age or surroundings.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Each nucleus has a decay probability λ dt in time dt, independent of other nuclei. For N nuclei: dN = −λN dt. This first-order ODE has solution N(t) = N₀ e^(−λt). The half-life t½ satisfies N(t½) = N₀/2: N₀/2 = N₀ e^(−λt½), giving t½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ. The constant-probability assumption follows from quantum mechanics: decay is a tunneling process whose rate depends only on the nuclear Hamiltonian.
equations.working_example: Carbon-14 dating: t½ = 5730 years, λ = 0.693/5730 = 1.21×10⁻⁴ yr⁻¹. A sample has 25% of original C-14. N/N₀ = 0.25 = e^(−λt), so t = −ln(0.25)/λ = 1.386/(1.21×10⁻⁴) = 11,460 years (exactly 2 half-lives, as expected for 25% remaining).
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations from pure exponential decay: (1) The quantum Zeno effect — very frequent measurements can slow decay. At very short times (t ≪ 1/λ), the decay probability is proportional to t² (not λt). (2) At very long times, the exponential law is replaced by a power law (inverse-power tail) due to the lower bound on energy eigenstates. (3) In dense environments (stellar interiors), electron capture rates change because the electron density at the nucleus is altered.
equations.description: The number of undecayed radioactive nuclei decreases exponentially over time. Each nucleus has a constant probability λ of decaying per unit time, independent of its age or surroundings. This is the basis for radiometric dating and nuclear medicine dosimetry.

equations.name: Nuclear Binding Energy
equations.domain_of_applicability: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy equivalent of the mass difference between its constituent nucleons and the assembled nucleus. Higher binding energy per nucleon means greater nuclear stability.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From E = mc²: if the nucleus has mass M less than the sum of its parts (Zm_p + Nm_n), the 'missing' mass Δm = Zm_p + Nm_n − M has been converted to binding energy B = Δmc². This energy was released when the nucleus formed and must be supplied to completely disassemble it. The semi-empirical mass formula (Bethe–Weizsäcker) models B as a sum of volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, and pairing terms.
equations.negation_failure_case: The simple formula does not account for nuclear shell effects. Nuclei with magic numbers (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) have anomalously high binding energies due to closed nuclear shells (analogous to noble gas electron shells). The semi-empirical mass formula overestimates the mass of doubly magic nuclei like He-4, O-16, Ca-40, and Pb-208 because it treats nuclear matter as a smooth liquid drop.
equations.source_citation: Aston, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A (1927)
equations.description: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy equivalent of the mass difference between its constituent nucleons and the assembled nucleus. Higher binding energy per nucleon means greater nuclear stability. The curve of B/A vs A explains why both fission (heavy nuclei) and fusion (light nuclei) release energy.

equations.name: Time Dilation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Moving clocks run slower as observed from a stationary frame. A time interval Δt measured in the rest frame of a clock appears dilated to γΔt in a frame where the clock moves at velocity v.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider a light clock: light bounces between two mirrors separated by distance d. In the rest frame, tick time is Δt₀ = 2d/c. In a frame where the clock moves at v, the light path is diagonal: 2√(d² + (vΔt/2)²) = cΔt. Squaring: 4d² + v²Δt² = c²Δt². Solving: Δt = 2d/(c√(1−v²/c²)) = γΔt₀.
equations.working_example: GPS satellite clocks (v ≈ 3,874 m/s): γ = 1/√(1 − (3874/3×10⁸)²) ≈ 1 + 8.35×10⁻¹¹. Over 24 hours, the satellite clock loses Δt = 86400 × 8.35×10⁻¹¹ × c ≈ 7.2 μs/day. Without correction, GPS positions would drift ~2.2 km/day.
equations.negation_failure_case: If time dilation is ignored in GPS: the SR contribution alone causes a 7.2 μs/day drift (positions off by ~2 km/day). Including GR (gravitational blueshift adds +45.9 μs/day), the net correction is ~38.7 μs/day. GPS would be useless within hours without relativistic corrections.
equations.description: Moving clocks run slower as observed from a stationary frame. A time interval Δt measured in the rest frame of a clock appears dilated to γΔt in a frame where the clock moves at velocity v. This has been confirmed by muon decay experiments, GPS satellite corrections, and particle accelerator lifetimes.

equations.name: Length Contraction
equations.domain_of_applicability: An object moving relative to an observer is measured to be shorter along the direction of motion by a factor of 1/γ. This is a real physical effect (not an optical illusion) arising from the relativity of simultaneity — the two ends of the object are measured at different events in different frames.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: In the object's rest frame, its length is L₀ = x₂ − x₁ measured at any time. In the lab frame (object moving at v), we measure both ends simultaneously (same t). Using the Lorentz transformation: x' = γ(x − vt). Setting t = 0 for both measurements: L₀ = x'₂ − x'₁ = γ(x₂ − x₁) = γL. Therefore L = L₀/γ.
equations.working_example: A spacecraft 100 m long in its rest frame travels at v = 0.8c. γ = 1/√(1−0.64) = 1/0.6 = 5/3. Observed length: L = 100/(5/3) = 60 m. The ship appears 40% shorter to a stationary observer.
equations.negation_failure_case: At v = 0.001c (300 km/s — fastest human-made objects), γ ≈ 1 + 5×10⁻⁷. Contraction of a 100 m rocket: ΔL = 0.05 μm — far below any measurement capability. Length contraction is undetectable at everyday speeds, which is why it was unknown before the 20th century.
equations.description: An object moving relative to an observer is measured to be shorter along the direction of motion by a factor of 1/γ. This is a real physical effect (not an optical illusion) arising from the relativity of simultaneity — the two ends of the object are measured at different events in different frames.

equations.name: Schwarzschild Radius
equations.domain_of_applicability: The radius of the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole. Any object compressed below its Schwarzschild radius forms a black hole from which nothing can escape.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From the Schwarzschild metric (exact vacuum solution of Einstein's field equations for spherical symmetry): ds² = −(1−2GM/(rc²))c²dt² + dr²/(1−2GM/(rc²)) + r²dΩ². The metric becomes singular (coordinate singularity) when g_tt = 0, i.e., 1 − 2GM/(rc²) = 0, giving r = r_s = 2GM/c². This is the event horizon: the escape velocity equals c.
equations.working_example: Black hole of M = 10 solar masses = 1.99×10³¹ kg: r_s = 2(6.674×10⁻¹¹)(1.99×10³¹)/(9×10¹⁶) = 29.5 km. The Sagittarius A* black hole (M ≈ 4×10⁶ M☉): r_s ≈ 1.2×10¹⁰ m ≈ 0.08 AU.
equations.negation_failure_case: Newtonian gravity gives the same formula for the 'escape velocity = c' radius, but this is coincidental. Newtonian theory incorrectly predicts that light could still escape (just be redshifted), while GR correctly predicts that nothing can escape because spacetime itself is curved inward. Additionally, for rotating black holes, the Schwarzschild formula is wrong — the Kerr metric gives r± = GM/c² ± √((GM/c²)² − a²), which can be significantly smaller.
equations.description: The radius of the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole. Any object compressed below its Schwarzschild radius forms a black hole from which nothing can escape. For the Sun, r_s ≈ 3 km; for Earth, r_s ≈ 9 mm.

equations.name: Arrhenius Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Describes the temperature dependence of reaction rate constants. Higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier, exponentially accelerating the reaction.
key_assumptions: (1) Enzyme-catalyzed reactions above optimal temperature — enzymes denature (unfold), and the rate drops precipitously despite higher T.
equations.derivation_summary: Arrhenius observed that ln k vs 1/T is linear for most reactions. From the Boltzmann distribution, the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ E_a is proportional to e^(−E_a/RT). The rate constant k = (collision frequency) × (fraction with sufficient energy) × (steric factor) = A e^(−E_a/RT). Transition state theory (Eyring, 1935) provides a more rigorous derivation: k = (k_BT/h) e^(−ΔG‡/RT), which reduces to Arrhenius form when the entropy of activation is temperature-independent.
equations.working_example: A reaction with E_a = 75 kJ/mol and A = 10¹³ s⁻¹. At T = 300 K: k = 10¹³ × e^(−75000/(8.314×300)) = 10¹³ × e^(−30.1) = 10¹³ × 8.5×10⁻¹⁴ = 0.85 s⁻¹. At T = 350 K: k = 10¹³ × e^(−25.8) = 10¹³ × 6.3×10⁻¹² = 63 s⁻¹. A 50 K increase speeds the reaction 74×.
equations.negation_failure_case: Fails for: (1) Enzyme-catalyzed reactions above optimal temperature — enzymes denature (unfold), and the rate drops precipitously despite higher T. (2) Quantum tunneling reactions (e.g., proton transfer in enzymes) where particles pass through the barrier rather than over it, showing weaker temperature dependence than Arrhenius predicts. (3) Non-Arrhenius curvature at very high or low temperatures due to changes in the reaction mechanism.
equations.description: Describes the temperature dependence of reaction rate constants. Higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier, exponentially accelerating the reaction. It is the most widely used equation in chemical kinetics.

equations.name: Nernst Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Gives the electrode potential under non-standard conditions by correcting the standard potential for the actual concentrations of reactants and products. It is fundamental to electrochemistry, battery design, corrosion science, and membrane biophysics.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The Gibbs free energy of a reaction is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. The electrical work done by an electrochemical cell is W = nFE = −ΔG. At standard conditions, nFE° = −ΔG°. Combining: nFE = nFE° − RT ln Q, giving E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q. At equilibrium (E = 0), this gives ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K.
equations.working_example: Zn/Cu cell at 25°C, [Zn²⁺] = 0.1 M, [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 M. E° = 1.10 V, n = 2. E = 1.10 − (0.02569/2)ln(0.1/1.0) = 1.10 − (0.01285)(−2.303) = 1.10 + 0.030 = 1.13 V. Higher Cu²⁺ concentration drives the cell potential above standard.
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations occur at: (1) High ionic strength where activities ≠ concentrations — the Debye–Hückel theory gives activity coefficients < 1 for most ions, modifying the effective Q. (2) Very high current densities where overpotentials (activation, concentration, ohmic) dominate and the equilibrium Nernst equation is irrelevant. (3) Non-reversible electrodes where kinetic barriers prevent equilibrium from being established.
equations.description: Gives the electrode potential under non-standard conditions by correcting the standard potential for the actual concentrations of reactants and products. It is fundamental to electrochemistry, battery design, corrosion science, and membrane biophysics.

equations.name: Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Relates the pH of a buffer solution to the acid dissociation constant and the ratio of conjugate base to acid concentrations. It is indispensable in biochemistry for designing buffers and understanding blood pH regulation.
key_assumptions: (1) The ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is extreme (< 0.
very dilute solutions.
equations.derivation_summary: Start from the equilibrium expression for a weak acid HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: K_a = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Take −log of both sides: −log K_a = −log[H⁺] − log([A⁻]/[HA]). Since pK_a = −log K_a and pH = −log[H⁺]: pK_a = pH − log([A⁻]/[HA]), rearranging to pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
equations.working_example: Acetate buffer: pK_a = 4.76, [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.15 M, [CH₃COOH] = 0.10 M. pH = 4.76 + log(0.15/0.10) = 4.76 + log(1.5) = 4.76 + 0.176 = 4.94. Adding 0.01 mol HCl to 1 L: new ratio = 0.14/0.11 = 1.27, pH = 4.76 + 0.105 = 4.87. The buffer resists pH change (only 0.07 units vs ~5 units for unbuffered water).
equations.negation_failure_case: Fails when: (1) The ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is extreme (< 0.1 or > 10), i.e., pH is more than 1 unit from pK_a — the buffer capacity is negligible. (2) Concentrations are very low — the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation assumes [A⁻] and [HA] are much larger than [H⁺], which fails in very dilute solutions. (3) The ionic strength is high — activity coefficients deviate from 1, and the equation should use activities rather than concentrations.
equations.description: Relates the pH of a buffer solution to the acid dissociation constant and the ratio of conjugate base to acid concentrations. It is indispensable in biochemistry for designing buffers and understanding blood pH regulation.

equations.name: Beer–Lambert Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The absorbance of a solution is proportional to the molar absorptivity of the solute, the path length, and the concentration. It is the quantitative basis for spectrophotometry and is used universally for determining concentrations in analytical chemistry, biochemistry, and clinical diagnostics.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider a beam of intensity I₀ passing through a thin slab of thickness dx containing absorbing molecules at concentration c. The fractional intensity decrease is dI/I = −αc dx, where α is an absorption coefficient. Integrating: I = I₀ e^(−αcl). Defining absorbance A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl, where ε = α/(2.303) is the molar absorptivity (L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹).
equations.working_example: NADH at 340 nm: ε = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, path length l = 1 cm, measured A = 0.45. Concentration: c = A/(εl) = 0.45/(6220 × 1) = 7.23 × 10⁻⁵ M = 72.3 μM.
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations from Beer's Law occur at: (1) High concentrations (> ~0.01 M) where solute–solute interactions alter ε. (2) Polychromatic light — if the light source has a range of wavelengths and ε varies with λ, the observed absorbance is not linear in c. (3) Fluorescent or scattering samples — emitted or scattered light reaches the detector, giving apparently lower absorbance. (4) Chemical equilibria that shift with concentration (e.g., dimerization) change the effective absorbing species.
equations.description: The absorbance of a solution is proportional to the molar absorptivity of the solute, the path length, and the concentration. It is the quantitative basis for spectrophotometry and is used universally for determining concentrations in analytical chemistry, biochemistry, and clinical diagnostics.

equations.name: van der Waals Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: A real gas equation of state that corrects the ideal gas law for intermolecular attractive forces (parameter a) and finite molecular volume (parameter b). It qualitatively predicts the liquid–gas phase transition and the existence of a critical point.
key_assumptions: Idealized conditions
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Start with the ideal gas law PV = RT (per mole). Correction 1: molecules have finite volume, reducing the available volume to V − b. Correction 2: intermolecular attractions reduce the pressure exerted on the walls by a/V² (proportional to the square of the number density n/V, since each molecule is attracted by its neighbors). Combining: (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT. The critical point satisfies dP/dV = 0 and d²P/dV² = 0, giving T_c = 8a/(27Rb), V_c = 3b, P_c = a/(27b²).
equations.working_example: CO₂ at T = 500 K, V = 0.5 L/mol: a = 3.59 L²·atm/mol², b = 0.0427 L/mol. P = RT/(V−b) − a/V² = (0.08206×500)/(0.5−0.0427) − 3.59/0.25 = 41.03/0.4573 − 14.36 = 89.7 − 14.4 = 75.3 atm. Ideal gas: P = RT/V = 82.06 atm. The real gas pressure is 8.3% lower due to attractive forces.
equations.negation_failure_case: Limitations: (1) The van der Waals equation is only semi-quantitative; it overestimates the critical compressibility factor (Z_c = PcVc/RTc = 3/8 = 0.375) compared to real gases (Z_c ≈ 0.23–0.29). (2) It cannot accurately describe the liquid phase or the phase boundary. (3) For strongly polar or hydrogen-bonding molecules (water, ammonia), more sophisticated equations (Peng–Robinson, SAFT) are needed because the a parameter is not constant.
equations.description: A real gas equation of state that corrects the ideal gas law for intermolecular attractive forces (parameter a) and finite molecular volume (parameter b). It qualitatively predicts the liquid–gas phase transition and the existence of a critical point.

equations.name: Equilibrium Constant Expression
equations.domain_of_applicability: At equilibrium, the ratio of product to reactant concentrations (each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients) is constant at a given temperature. K determines the position of equilibrium and connects to thermodynamics via ΔG° = −RT ln K.
key_assumptions: System at or near equilibrium
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: For a general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, at equilibrium ΔG = 0. From ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, setting ΔG = 0 gives Q_eq = K = e^(−ΔG°/RT). From chemical kinetics: at equilibrium, the forward rate r_f = k_f[A]^a[B]^b equals the reverse rate r_r = k_r[C]^c[D]^d, giving K = k_f/k_r = [C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b).
equations.working_example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, K = 6.0×10⁵ at 298 K. If [N₂] = 1 M, [H₂] = 1 M at equilibrium: [NH₃]² = K[N₂][H₂]³ = 6×10⁵. [NH₃] = 775 M (unrealistic — shows the reaction overwhelmingly favors products at 298 K, though kinetics are very slow without a catalyst).
equations.negation_failure_case: K is only valid at equilibrium and at the specific temperature. (1) If the system is not at equilibrium, Q ≠ K and the reaction shifts toward equilibrium. (2) K changes with temperature via the van't Hoff equation: d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²). For the Haber process, at 700 K, K drops to ~0.006 — vastly less favorable. (3) Using concentrations instead of activities gives incorrect K values for non-ideal solutions.
equations.description: At equilibrium, the ratio of product to reactant concentrations (each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients) is constant at a given temperature. K determines the position of equilibrium and connects to thermodynamics via ΔG° = −RT ln K.

equations.name: Hess's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path. Reaction enthalpies can be calculated by combining the standard enthalpies of formation of products and reactants.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Since H is a state function (depends only on state, not path), ΔH for a reaction is path-independent. Any reaction can be decomposed into: (1) decomposing reactants into their elements in standard states (−ΣΔH_f(reactants)), then (2) forming products from elements (ΣΔH_f(products)). The total is ΔH_rxn = ΣΔH_f(products) − ΣΔH_f(reactants).
equations.working_example: Combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. ΔH_f values (kJ/mol): CH₄ = −74.8, O₂ = 0, CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8. ΔH = [−393.5 + 2(−285.8)] − [−74.8 + 0] = −965.1 + 74.8 = −890.3 kJ/mol. This matches calorimetric measurements.
equations.negation_failure_case: Hess's Law requires that all ΔH_f values be at the same conditions (usually 25°C, 1 atm). Using ΔH_f at different temperatures without heat capacity corrections gives incorrect results. For reactions where temperature varies significantly (e.g., combustion at 2000°C), Kirchhoff's equation ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ∫ΔC_p dT must be applied.
equations.description: The enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path. Reaction enthalpies can be calculated by combining the standard enthalpies of formation of products and reactants. This is a direct consequence of enthalpy being a state function.

equations.name: Bragg's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The condition for constructive X-ray diffraction from crystal lattice planes. It relates the X-ray wavelength, interplanar spacing, and angle of incidence.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider X-rays reflecting from two adjacent parallel lattice planes separated by distance d. The lower beam travels an extra path length of 2d sinθ compared to the upper beam (derived from geometry: the extra distance is d sinθ before and after the reflection point). Constructive interference occurs when this path difference equals an integer number of wavelengths: 2d sinθ = nλ.
equations.working_example: Cu Kα X-rays (λ = 1.5406 Å) diffract from NaCl (d = 2.82 Å). First-order (n=1) diffraction angle: sinθ = λ/(2d) = 1.5406/(2×2.82) = 0.273, θ = 15.86°. Second-order (n=2): sinθ = 2(1.5406)/(2×2.82) = 0.547, θ = 33.1°.
equations.negation_failure_case: Bragg's Law gives only the positions of diffraction peaks, not their intensities. The structure factor (which depends on the electron density and atomic positions within the unit cell) determines intensities and can cause 'systematic absences' where Bragg's condition is met but the diffraction peak vanishes due to destructive interference between atoms within the basis. Additionally, for amorphous materials (glass, liquids), there are no well-defined planes and Bragg's Law does not apply.
equations.source_citation: Bragg, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A (1913)
equations.description: The condition for constructive X-ray diffraction from crystal lattice planes. It relates the X-ray wavelength, interplanar spacing, and angle of incidence. It is the foundation of X-ray crystallography, which has determined the structures of millions of molecules including DNA and proteins.

equations.name: Raoult's Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The partial vapor pressure of a component in an ideal solution equals its mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure. It describes how mixing reduces vapor pressure and is the basis for understanding boiling-point elevation and colligative properties.
key_assumptions: non-ideal solutions.
equations.derivation_summary: In an ideal solution, the chemical potential of component A is μ_A = μ°_A + RT ln x_A. At vapor-liquid equilibrium, μ_A(liquid) = μ_A(vapor). For pure A: μ°_A(l) = μ°_A(g) + RT ln P°_A. For the mixture: μ°_A(l) + RT ln x_A = μ°_A(g) + RT ln P_A. Subtracting: RT ln x_A = RT ln(P_A/P°_A), giving P_A = x_A P°_A.
equations.working_example: Benzene (P° = 100 torr) and toluene (P° = 40 torr) mixture, x_benzene = 0.6, x_toluene = 0.4. P_total = 0.6(100) + 0.4(40) = 60 + 16 = 76 torr.
equations.negation_failure_case: Fails for non-ideal solutions. Ethanol-water mixture at x_ethanol = 0.5: Raoult's law predicts P = 0.5(58.9) = 29.5 torr. Actual P ≈ 48 torr (positive deviation due to disrupted hydrogen bonding). The deviation is so large that an azeotrope forms at x ≈ 0.89.
equations.description: The partial vapor pressure of a component in an ideal solution equals its mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure. It describes how mixing reduces vapor pressure and is the basis for understanding boiling-point elevation and colligative properties.

equations.name: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
equations.domain_of_applicability: The mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, the molar mass of the substance, and inversely proportional to the number of electrons transferred per ion. This connects electrochemistry to stoichiometry.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The charge needed to deposit one mole of a substance requiring n electrons per ion is Q = nF (where F = N_A e = 96,485 C/mol). For an arbitrary charge Q, the moles deposited are Q/(nF), and the mass is m = Q M/(nF).
equations.working_example: Electroplating copper (M = 63.55 g/mol, n = 2) with I = 5 A for t = 3600 s: Q = It = 18,000 C. m = (18,000)(63.55)/(2×96,485) = 5.93 g of copper deposited.
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations occur when: (1) Side reactions consume charge (hydrogen evolution competes with metal deposition, reducing current efficiency from 100% to perhaps 60-90%). (2) Non-uniform current distribution causes uneven deposition. (3) At very high current densities, mass transport limitations cause concentration polarization, and the relationship between charge and mass becomes nonlinear.
equations.description: The mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, the molar mass of the substance, and inversely proportional to the number of electrons transferred per ion. This connects electrochemistry to stoichiometry.

equations.name: Michaelis–Menten Kinetics
equations.domain_of_applicability: Describes the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reactions as a function of substrate concentration. At low [S], the rate is approximately linear; at high [S], the rate saturates at V_max.
key_assumptions: (1) Allosteric enzymes with cooperative binding — the Hill equation v = V_max[S]^n/(K^n + [S]^n) is needed (e.
equations.derivation_summary: For the reaction scheme E + S ⇌ ES → E + P with rate constants k₁, k⁻₁, k₂. The steady-state assumption (d[ES]/dt = 0) gives k₁[E][S] = (k⁻₁ + k₂)[ES]. Since [E]_total = [E] + [ES]: [ES] = [E]_total[S]/(K_m + [S]) where K_m = (k⁻₁ + k₂)/k₁. The reaction velocity v = k₂[ES] = k₂[E]_total[S]/(K_m + [S]) = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]).
equations.working_example: An enzyme with V_max = 100 μmol/min and K_m = 5 mM. At [S] = 1 mM: v = 100(1)/(5+1) = 16.7 μmol/min. At [S] = 5 mM (= K_m): v = 100(5)/10 = 50 μmol/min (half V_max). At [S] = 50 mM: v = 100(50)/55 = 90.9 μmol/min (91% of V_max).
equations.negation_failure_case: Fails for: (1) Allosteric enzymes with cooperative binding — the Hill equation v = V_max[S]^n/(K^n + [S]^n) is needed (e.g., ATCase shows sigmoidal kinetics with n ≈ 2.5). (2) Substrate inhibition — at very high [S], some enzymes slow down because substrate binds a second site, creating a dead-end complex. (3) Multi-substrate enzymes — most enzymes use 2+ substrates, requiring more complex kinetic models (ping-pong, ordered sequential).
equations.description: Describes the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reactions as a function of substrate concentration. At low [S], the rate is approximately linear; at high [S], the rate saturates at V_max. K_m is the substrate concentration at half-maximum velocity and reflects the enzyme's affinity for its substrate.

equations.name: Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium
equations.domain_of_applicability: In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration, or genetic drift, allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations. It provides the null hypothesis for population genetics: deviations indicate evolutionary forces at work.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider a gene with two alleles A (frequency p) and a (frequency q = 1−p). Under random mating, the probability of each genotype in the next generation is: P(AA) = p², P(Aa) = 2pq, P(aa) = q². The allele frequency in the next generation: p' = p² + ½(2pq) = p² + pq = p(p+q) = p. Therefore p is unchanged from one generation to the next, and so are the genotype frequencies. Equilibrium is reached in a single generation of random mating.
equations.working_example: Cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive): disease frequency = q² = 1/2500 = 0.0004 in European populations. Then q = 0.02, p = 0.98. Carrier frequency: 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.0392 ≈ 1 in 25 people. This explains why a rare disease has a surprisingly high carrier rate.
equations.negation_failure_case: Violations reveal evolutionary forces: (1) Selection — sickle cell trait: in malaria-endemic regions, heterozygotes (Aa) have higher fitness than either homozygote, maintaining q ≈ 0.1 despite aa being lethal. HW would predict q should decrease. (2) Genetic drift in small populations — founder effects in Amish communities cause Ellis–van Creveld syndrome at 5× expected frequency. (3) Non-random mating (assortative mating, inbreeding) increases homozygosity beyond HW predictions.
equations.description: In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration, or genetic drift, allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations. It provides the null hypothesis for population genetics: deviations indicate evolutionary forces at work.

equations.name: Logistic Growth Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Models population growth that slows as the population approaches its carrying capacity K. Unlike exponential growth, resources limit the population.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Start with exponential growth dN/dt = rN. Add a density-dependent factor (1 − N/K) that reduces the growth rate linearly as N approaches K. When N ≪ K, growth is approximately exponential. When N = K, growth stops. When N > K, the population declines. The analytical solution is N(t) = K/(1 + ((K−N₀)/N₀)e^(−rt)).
equations.negation_failure_case: Limitations: (1) Real populations overshoot K then oscillate or crash — not captured by the smooth logistic curve. Deer on islands frequently exhibit boom–bust dynamics. (2) Time delays in reproduction cause oscillations: the delayed logistic dN/dt = rN(t)(1 − N(t−τ)/K) can produce chaos for rτ > π/2. (3) The Allee effect (reduced growth at very low N due to mate-finding difficulty) causes extinction thresholds absent in the logistic model.
equations.description: Models population growth that slows as the population approaches its carrying capacity K. Unlike exponential growth, resources limit the population. This produces an S-shaped (sigmoidal) growth curve seen in bacteria, animals, and human populations approaching resource limits.

equations.name: Lotka–Volterra Equations
equations.formula: dx/dt = αx − βxy; dy/dt = δxy − γy
equations.symbols: dx/dt = αx − βxy; dy/dt = δxy − γy
equations.domain_of_applicability: Coupled differential equations modeling predator–prey population dynamics. Prey grow exponentially but are consumed by predators; predators grow in proportion to prey consumed but die naturally.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The equations are constructed from ecological assumptions: prey (x) grow at rate αx minus predation βxy (proportional to encounter rate). Predators (y) grow from consumed prey at rate δxy minus natural death γy. The system has equilibria at (0,0) and (x* = γ/δ, y* = α/β). Linearization around the nontrivial equilibrium gives eigenvalues ±i√(αγ), confirming neutral oscillations with period T = 2π/√(αγ). The conserved quantity is H = δx − γ ln x + βy − α ln y.
equations.working_example: Hares (α = 1.0, β = 0.1) and lynx (γ = 0.5, δ = 0.02). Equilibrium: x* = 0.5/0.02 = 25 hares, y* = 1.0/0.1 = 10 lynx. Period: T = 2π/√(1.0×0.5) = 8.89 time units. Starting at x = 40, y = 5: prey overshoot drives predator increase, which then crashes prey, completing the cycle.
equations.negation_failure_case: Major failures: (1) The basic model predicts neutral cycles (constant amplitude forever), but real populations show damped or limit-cycle oscillations due to density dependence not included in the model. (2) Stochastic extinction: with small populations, random fluctuations can drive either species extinct (the model predicts infinite populations can revive from arbitrarily small numbers). (3) Functional response saturation — real predators cannot consume unlimited prey; the Holling type II/III functional response is more realistic.
equations.description: Coupled differential equations modeling predator–prey population dynamics. Prey grow exponentially but are consumed by predators; predators grow in proportion to prey consumed but die naturally. The model predicts cyclic population oscillations, as observed in lynx–hare data.

equations.name: SIR Model (Epidemiology)
equations.formula: dS/dt = −βSI; dI/dt = βSI − γI; dR/dt = γI
equations.symbols: dS/dt = −βSI; dI/dt = βSI − γI; dR/dt = γI
equations.domain_of_applicability: The foundational compartmental model for infectious disease spread. The population is divided into Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered compartments.
key_assumptions: (1) Diseases with significant pre-symptomatic/asymptomatic transmission (COVID-19) — SEIR (adding Exposed compartment) is needed.
equations.derivation_summary: Assumptions: (1) Homogeneous mixing: each individual contacts others at rate β. (2) Infected recover at rate γ. Mass action: new infections = βSI (proportional to product of S and I). Recoveries = γI. The basic reproduction number R₀ = βS₀/γ determines epidemic threshold: if R₀ > 1, an epidemic occurs; if R₀ < 1, the disease dies out. The final size equation: ln(S∞/S₀) = −R₀(1 − S∞/N).
equations.working_example: Measles: R₀ = 15, γ = 1/10 days, so β = R₀γ/N. In a population of 100,000 with 99,999 susceptible and 1 infected: herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R₀ = 1 − 1/15 = 93.3%. Final epidemic size (unvaccinated): solving the transcendental equation gives S∞/N ≈ 0.00001, meaning ~99.999% of the population is infected.
equations.negation_failure_case: SIR fails for: (1) Diseases with significant pre-symptomatic/asymptomatic transmission (COVID-19) — SEIR (adding Exposed compartment) is needed. (2) Heterogeneous contact networks (superspreaders) — network models show that overdispersed transmission (80/20 rule) dramatically changes epidemic dynamics. (3) Waning immunity — for diseases like influenza where R→S transitions occur, the SIRS model produces endemic oscillations.
equations.source_citation: Kermack & McKendrick, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A (1927)
equations.description: The foundational compartmental model for infectious disease spread. The population is divided into Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered compartments. It predicts epidemic thresholds, peak infection timing, and final epidemic size. It was central to modeling COVID-19.

equations.name: Fick's Laws of Diffusion
equations.domain_of_applicability: Fick's First Law states that diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient. Fick's Second Law describes how concentration changes over time due to diffusion.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: First Law: consider a plane at position x. The net flux of particles is proportional to the concentration gradient — more particles move from high to low concentration. Dimensionally, J [mol/(m²·s)] = −D [m²/s] × dC/dx [mol/m⁴]. Second Law: apply conservation of mass to a slab of thickness dx: ∂C/∂t × dx = J(x) − J(x+dx) = −(∂J/∂x)dx. Substituting J = −D∂C/∂x: ∂C/∂t = D∂²C/∂x².
equations.working_example: Oxygen diffusing across an alveolar membrane: D = 2.1×10⁻⁵ cm²/s, thickness = 0.5 μm = 5×10⁻⁵ cm, ΔC = 8 mmol/L = 8×10⁻⁶ mol/cm³. Flux: J = DΔC/Δx = (2.1×10⁻⁵)(8×10⁻⁶)/(5×10⁻⁵) = 3.36×10⁻⁶ mol/(cm²·s). Over total alveolar surface area (~70 m²): total O₂ transfer = 235 mL/min, matching measured values.
equations.negation_failure_case: Fick's Laws fail when: (1) Concentration is very high and molecular crowding matters — the diffusion coefficient D becomes concentration-dependent. (2) Active transport is present — biological membranes use ATP-driven pumps that move molecules against the concentration gradient, violating J ∝ −dC/dx. (3) Anomalous diffusion in crowded cellular environments where <x²> ∝ t^α with α ≠ 1 (subdiffusion in cytoplasm, α ≈ 0.7).
equations.description: Fick's First Law states that diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient. Fick's Second Law describes how concentration changes over time due to diffusion. These govern molecular transport in biology (oxygen diffusion in lungs), chemistry (mixing), and materials science (doping semiconductors).

equations.name: Allometric Scaling
equations.domain_of_applicability: Biological variables scale with body mass raised to a power. Metabolic rate scales as M^(3/4) (Kleiber's Law), lifespan as M^(1/4), and heart rate as M^(−1/4).
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: West, Brown, and Enquist (1997) derived the 3/4 exponent from fractal-like branching networks that distribute resources (blood vessels, bronchial tubes). They assumed: (1) the network fills the entire body (space-filling), (2) terminal branch units (capillaries) are invariant across species, (3) the network minimizes transport energy. These three constraints yield metabolic rate B ∝ M^(3/4). The derivation uses the scaling of pipe radii, lengths, and branching ratios through hierarchical levels.
equations.working_example: Mouse (M = 0.02 kg): B = 70 × 0.02^0.75 = 70 × 0.0335 = 2.35 W = 203 kcal/day. Elephant (M = 4000 kg): B = 70 × 4000^0.75 = 70 × 565 = 39,500 W. Per kg: mouse = 117 W/kg, elephant = 9.9 W/kg. Smaller animals have ~12× higher mass-specific metabolic rates.
equations.negation_failure_case: Deviations: (1) The exact exponent is debated — some analyses find b = 2/3 (surface area scaling) rather than 3/4 for certain taxa. (2) Endotherms and ectotherms have different normalization constants Y₀ even with the same exponent. (3) Individual variation within species is large (±30%), and the scaling law applies statistically across species, not predictively for individuals.
equations.source_citation: Kleiber, Hilgardia (1932); West et al., Science (1997)
equations.description: Biological variables scale with body mass raised to a power. Metabolic rate scales as M^(3/4) (Kleiber's Law), lifespan as M^(1/4), and heart rate as M^(−1/4). These power laws span 21 orders of magnitude from bacteria to whales.

equations.name: Goldman Equation
equations.formula: V_m = (RT/F) ln[(P_K[K]_o + P_Na[Na]_o + P_Cl[Cl]_i) / (P_K[K]_i + P_Na[Na]_i + P_Cl[Cl]_o)]
equations.symbols: V_m = (RT/F) ln[(P_K[K]_o + P_Na[Na]_o + P_Cl[Cl]_i) / (P_K[K]_i + P_Na[Na]_i + P_Cl[Cl]_o)]
equations.domain_of_applicability: Calculates the resting membrane potential considering multiple ion species and their relative permeabilities. It generalizes the Nernst equation (single ion) to real membranes where K⁺, Na⁺, and Cl⁻ all contribute.
key_assumptions: (1) The membrane has significant fixed charges that distort the field.
equations.derivation_summary: Assume constant electric field across the membrane (Goldman's constant-field approximation). For each ion species, solve the Nernst-Planck equation (flux = diffusion + drift) under steady-state conditions. The voltage at which net current is zero gives the Goldman equation. The derivation requires integrating the flux equations across the membrane thickness with the constant-field assumption.
equations.negation_failure_case: The constant-field assumption fails when: (1) The membrane has significant fixed charges that distort the field. (2) Ion channels are clustered, creating non-uniform field distributions. (3) Electrogenic pumps (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) contribute directly to V_m by pumping 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, adding ~−3 to −10 mV that the Goldman equation doesn't capture.
equations.description: Calculates the resting membrane potential considering multiple ion species and their relative permeabilities. It generalizes the Nernst equation (single ion) to real membranes where K⁺, Na⁺, and Cl⁻ all contribute.

equations.name: Basic Reproduction Number
equations.domain_of_applicability: The average number of secondary infections produced by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population. If R₀ > 1, an epidemic occurs; if R₀ < 1, the disease dies out.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: From the SIR model: dI/dt = βSI/N − γI. At the start (S ≈ N): dI/dt = (β − γ)I. The epidemic grows if β > γ, i.e., R₀ = β/γ > 1. Alternatively: an infected individual transmits at rate βS₀/N per unit time and remains infectious for average time 1/γ, producing R₀ = βS₀/(Nγ) ≈ β/γ secondary cases.
equations.working_example: COVID-19 (original strain): β ≈ 0.4/day, γ ≈ 0.14/day. R₀ = 0.4/0.14 = 2.86. Herd immunity threshold: 1 − 1/2.86 = 65%. Delta variant: R₀ ≈ 5–8, requiring 80–87.5% immunity.
equations.negation_failure_case: R₀ is misleading when: (1) Transmission is overdispersed (superspreading) — SARS-CoV-2 had ~10% of cases causing ~80% of transmission, so the mean R₀ understates the importance of superspreading events while overstating the risk from typical cases. (2) The population is not homogeneously mixing (network structure matters). (3) Behavior changes during an epidemic reduce the effective R below R₀.
equations.description: The average number of secondary infections produced by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population. If R₀ > 1, an epidemic occurs; if R₀ < 1, the disease dies out. The herd immunity threshold is 1 − 1/R₀.

equations.name: Hill Equation
equations.domain_of_applicability: Describes cooperative ligand binding where the binding curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic. The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity: n > 1 is positive cooperativity (binding to one site facilitates binding to others), n = 1 reduces to Michaelis-Menten, n < 1 is negative cooperativity.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Hill assumed n ligands bind simultaneously: P + nL ⇌ PL_n with K_d = [P][L]^n/[PL_n]. Fractional saturation: θ = [PL_n]/([P]+[PL_n]) = [L]^n/(K_d^n + [L]^n). This is a phenomenological model — real binding is sequential, not simultaneous — but n captures the steepness of the binding curve and provides a useful empirical summary of cooperativity.
equations.working_example: Hemoglobin oxygen binding: n = 2.8, K_d corresponds to P₅₀ = 26 mmHg. At P_O₂ = 100 mmHg (lungs): θ = 100^2.8/(26^2.8 + 100^2.8) = 0.975 (97.5% saturated). At P_O₂ = 40 mmHg (tissues): θ = 40^2.8/(26^2.8 + 40^2.8) = 0.75 (75%). The steep curve enables efficient O₂ delivery.
equations.negation_failure_case: With n = 1 (no cooperativity, Michaelis-Menten): at 100 mmHg θ = 100/126 = 79%, at 40 mmHg θ = 40/66 = 61%. The difference is only 18% vs 22.5% for cooperative binding. Without cooperativity, hemoglobin would deliver 35% less oxygen to tissues per pass through circulation, which would be insufficient for aerobic metabolism.
equations.description: Describes cooperative ligand binding where the binding curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic. The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity: n > 1 is positive cooperativity (binding to one site facilitates binding to others), n = 1 reduces to Michaelis-Menten, n < 1 is negative cooperativity.

equations.name: Euler's Identity
equations.domain_of_applicability: Connects five fundamental mathematical constants (e, i, π, 1, 0) in a single equation. It is a special case of Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x at x = π.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Euler's formula: from the Taylor series: e^(ix) = Σ (ix)^n/n! = (1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − ...) + i(x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − ...) = cos x + i sin x. Substituting x = π: e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1 + 0 = −1. Therefore e^(iπ) + 1 = 0.
equations.working_example: Verify numerically: e^(iπ) = e^(3.14159i). Using the series to 10 terms: cos(3.14159) = −0.99999999... and sin(3.14159) = 0.00000265... ≈ 0. So e^(iπ) = −1.000 + 0.000i. Adding 1: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0.000.
equations.negation_failure_case: Euler's Identity is an exact mathematical truth, not an empirical law, so it cannot 'fail.' However, its derivation depends on: (1) the standard definition of exponentiation for complex numbers, (2) the convergence of Taylor series, and (3) the Archimedean property of real numbers. In non-standard analysis or p-adic number systems, the analogs of e, π, and i have different relationships.
equations.description: Connects five fundamental mathematical constants (e, i, π, 1, 0) in a single equation. It is a special case of Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x at x = π. Often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics, it bridges exponential, trigonometric, and complex analysis.

equations.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
equations.domain_of_applicability: Links differentiation and integration as inverse operations. The definite integral of a function equals its antiderivative evaluated at the bounds.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Part 1: Define F(x) = ∫_a^x f(t)dt. By the definition of the derivative: F'(x) = lim_{h→0} [F(x+h)−F(x)]/h = lim_{h→0} (1/h)∫_x^{x+h} f(t)dt. By the Mean Value Theorem for integrals, this equals f(c) for some c ∈ [x, x+h]. As h → 0, c → x, so F'(x) = f(x). Part 2: If G is any antiderivative of f (G' = f), then G = F + C. So ∫_a^b f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) = G(b) − G(a).
equations.working_example: Compute ∫₀³ x² dx. Antiderivative: F(x) = x³/3. F(3) − F(0) = 27/3 − 0 = 9. Verification by Riemann sum with n = 1000: Σ_{i=1}^{1000} (3i/1000)² × (3/1000) = 9.000013 ≈ 9.
equations.negation_failure_case: The theorem requires f to be Riemann-integrable. Pathological functions like: (1) f(x) = 1/√x on [0,1] (improper integral — the theorem extends to improper integrals but requires care). (2) The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not Riemann-integrable, so the FTC does not apply (though it is Lebesgue-integrable with integral 0). (3) F may not be differentiable everywhere — the Cantor function is continuous and F' = 0 a.e., yet F(1)−F(0) = 1 ≠ ∫₀¹ 0 dx.
equations.description: Links differentiation and integration as inverse operations. The definite integral of a function equals its antiderivative evaluated at the bounds. This is the most important theorem in calculus, enabling the analytical computation of areas, volumes, and accumulated quantities.

equations.name: Bayes' Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: Updates the probability of a hypothesis given new evidence. It inverts conditional probabilities: from P(evidence|hypothesis) to P(hypothesis|evidence).
key_assumptions: correlated features (e.
equations.derivation_summary: From the definition of conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) and P(B|A) = P(A∩B)/P(A). From the second: P(A∩B) = P(B|A)P(A). Substituting into the first: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). For total probability: P(B) = P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|A')P(A').
equations.working_example: Medical screening: disease prevalence P(D) = 0.01 (1%). Test sensitivity P(+|D) = 0.95, false positive rate P(+|D') = 0.05. P(D|+) = (0.95)(0.01)/[(0.95)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99)] = 0.0095/0.0590 = 0.161 = 16.1%. Despite 95% test accuracy, a positive result only means 16% chance of disease — the base rate fallacy.
equations.negation_failure_case: Bayes' theorem is mathematically exact but can be misapplied: (1) Wrong priors — if P(D) is set to 0 (dogmatic prior), no amount of evidence can change the posterior. (2) Assuming independence when events are correlated — the 'naive' in Naive Bayes assumes feature independence, which fails for correlated features (e.g., word co-occurrences in spam filtering). (3) Confusion of P(A|B) with P(B|A) — the 'prosecutor's fallacy' (P(evidence|innocent) ≠ P(innocent|evidence)).
equations.description: Updates the probability of a hypothesis given new evidence. It inverts conditional probabilities: from P(evidence|hypothesis) to P(hypothesis|evidence). It is the foundation of Bayesian statistics, machine learning, medical diagnosis, and spam filtering.

equations.name: Fourier Transform
equations.domain_of_applicability: Decomposes a time-domain signal into its constituent frequencies. It is arguably the most important mathematical tool in physics, engineering, and signal processing, enabling spectral analysis, filtering, image compression (JPEG), and solving differential equations.
key_assumptions: (frequencies above f_s/2 are misidentified).
equations.derivation_summary: Start with the Fourier series for a periodic function of period T: f(t) = Σ c_n e^(inω₀t) where c_n = (1/T)∫ f(t)e^(−inω₀t)dt. As T → ∞ (non-periodic functions), the discrete frequencies nω₀ become continuous ω, the sum becomes an integral, and c_n → F(ω)dω/(2π). The result is the Fourier transform pair: F(ω) = ∫ f(t)e^(−iωt)dt and the inverse f(t) = (1/2π)∫ F(ω)e^(iωt)dω.
equations.working_example: A Gaussian pulse f(t) = e^(−t²/2σ²): F(ω) = σ√(2π) e^(−σ²ω²/2). For σ = 1 ms: the frequency spectrum is also a Gaussian centered at ω = 0 with width Δω = 1/σ = 1000 rad/s. Narrow time pulse → broad frequency spectrum (uncertainty principle).
equations.negation_failure_case: The Fourier transform has limitations: (1) It assumes stationarity — for signals whose frequency content changes over time (speech, music), the short-time Fourier transform or wavelet transform is needed. (2) It does not exist for functions that grow without bound (e.g., f(t) = t) — the Laplace transform handles such functions. (3) Discrete sampling introduces aliasing if the sampling theorem is violated (frequencies above f_s/2 are misidentified).
equations.source_citation: Fourier, Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822)
equations.description: Decomposes a time-domain signal into its constituent frequencies. It is arguably the most important mathematical tool in physics, engineering, and signal processing, enabling spectral analysis, filtering, image compression (JPEG), and solving differential equations.

equations.name: Central Limit Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: The sampling distribution of the mean of any i.i.
key_assumptions: (1) Variance is infinite — Cauchy-distributed variables (σ = ∞) have a sample mean that is also Cauchy, never converging to normal.
equations.derivation_summary: Use characteristic functions: φ_X(t) = E[e^(itX)]. For the standardized sum Z_n = (ΣX_i − nμ)/(σ√n): φ_{Z_n}(t) = [φ_{(X-μ)/σ}(t/√n)]^n. Expand the characteristic function: φ_{(X-μ)/σ}(t/√n) = 1 − t²/(2n) + o(1/n). Then φ_{Z_n}(t) = [1 − t²/(2n)]^n → e^(−t²/2) as n→∞, which is the characteristic function of N(0,1). By Lévy's continuity theorem, Z_n → N(0,1).
equations.working_example: Roll a fair die (uniform on {1,...,6}, μ = 3.5, σ = 1.708). For n = 30 rolls, the sample mean has distribution approximately N(3.5, 1.708/√30) = N(3.5, 0.312). P(̄X > 4) = P(Z > (4−3.5)/0.312) = P(Z > 1.60) = 0.055 (5.5%). Despite the original uniform distribution, the sample mean is well-approximated by a Gaussian.
equations.negation_failure_case: The CLT fails when: (1) Variance is infinite — Cauchy-distributed variables (σ = ∞) have a sample mean that is also Cauchy, never converging to normal. Financial returns exhibit 'fat tails' where the CLT converges very slowly (if at all). (2) Variables are not independent — correlated observations (time series, spatial data) require modified CLT versions. (3) The sample size is too small for highly skewed distributions — n = 5 is insufficient for exponential data; n > 40 may be needed.
equations.description: The sampling distribution of the mean of any i.i.d. random variables with finite variance approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the underlying population distribution. This is why the normal distribution is ubiquitous in statistics and nature.

equations.name: Pythagorean Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: The sum of squares of the two legs of a right triangle equals the square of the hypotenuse. This is arguably the most fundamental theorem in geometry, with applications spanning surveying, navigation, physics, and computer graphics.
key_assumptions: on curved surfaces.
equations.derivation_summary: Proof by rearrangement (one of over 400 known proofs): construct a large square of side (a+b). Arrange four copies of the right triangle inside it, forming an inner tilted square of side c. Area of outer square: (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Area also equals: inner square + four triangles = c² + 4(½ab) = c² + 2ab. Therefore a² + 2ab + b² = c² + 2ab, giving a² + b² = c².
equations.working_example: Right triangle with legs a = 3, b = 4: c = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Distance from origin to point (5, 12): d = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13.
equations.negation_failure_case: The theorem fails on curved surfaces. On a sphere of radius R, a right triangle with legs a, b has hypotenuse c satisfying cos(c/R) = cos(a/R)cos(b/R) (spherical law of cosines). For a = b = πR/4 (quarter-circumference): cos(c/R) = cos²(π/4) = 1/2, giving c = Rπ/3. Euclidean prediction: c = πR√2/4 ≈ 1.11R. Spherical result: c = 1.047R. The 6% discrepancy is measurable for large-scale geodesy.
equations.description: The sum of squares of the two legs of a right triangle equals the square of the hypotenuse. This is arguably the most fundamental theorem in geometry, with applications spanning surveying, navigation, physics, and computer graphics.

equations.name: Taylor Series
equations.domain_of_applicability: Represents any smooth function as an infinite sum of polynomial terms about a point. It is the most important approximation tool in mathematics and physics, enabling linearization, numerical methods, and perturbation theory.
key_assumptions: (1) The function is not analytic — f(x) = e^(−1/x²) for x ≠ 0 (f(0) = 0) has all derivatives equal to zero at x = 0, so the Taylor series is identically 0, but f(x) > 0 everywhere else.
equations.derivation_summary: Define R_n(x) = f(x) − Σ_{k=0}^{n} f^(k)(a)(x−a)^k/k!. By repeated integration by parts (or the Mean Value Theorem generalization): R_n(x) = (1/n!)∫_a^x (x−t)^n f^(n+1)(t)dt. If f^(n+1) is bounded, R_n → 0 as n → ∞, and the series converges to f(x).
equations.working_example: Approximate e^0.1 using Taylor series about a = 0: e^x = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6 + ... For x = 0.1: e^0.1 ≈ 1 + 0.1 + 0.005 + 0.000167 = 1.10517. Exact value: 1.10517... The 4-term approximation is accurate to 6 decimal places.
equations.negation_failure_case: Taylor series fails when: (1) The function is not analytic — f(x) = e^(−1/x²) for x ≠ 0 (f(0) = 0) has all derivatives equal to zero at x = 0, so the Taylor series is identically 0, but f(x) > 0 everywhere else. (2) Outside the radius of convergence — 1/(1+x²) has Taylor series that diverges for |x| > 1 because of complex poles at x = ±i.
equations.description: Represents any smooth function as an infinite sum of polynomial terms about a point. It is the most important approximation tool in mathematics and physics, enabling linearization, numerical methods, and perturbation theory.

equations.name: Laplace Transform
equations.domain_of_applicability: Converts a time-domain function into the complex frequency domain, transforming differential equations into algebraic equations. It is the primary tool for analyzing linear systems, control theory, and circuit analysis.
key_assumptions: Linear regime / small perturbations
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: The Laplace transform is defined as an integral transform. Its key property for ODEs: L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0). This converts derivatives into multiplication by s. For a linear ODE a_n y^(n) + ... + a_0 y = g(t), applying L to both sides gives a polynomial in s times Y(s) = G(s) + initial condition terms, making the solution algebraic.
equations.negation_failure_case: The Laplace transform requires f(t) to grow no faster than exponentially (f(t) = O(e^{ct}) for some c). Functions like f(t) = e^{t²} grow too fast — the integral diverges for all s. Additionally, nonlinear ODEs cannot be solved by Laplace transform because L{f(y)} ≠ F(Y(s)) in general.
equations.description: Converts a time-domain function into the complex frequency domain, transforming differential equations into algebraic equations. It is the primary tool for analyzing linear systems, control theory, and circuit analysis.

equations.name: Stokes' Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: The line integral of a vector field around a closed curve equals the surface integral of its curl over any surface bounded by that curve. It generalizes Green's theorem to 3D and unifies all fundamental theorems of vector calculus under the framework of differential forms.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: For a smooth surface S bounded by curve C with unit normal n: parametrize S as r(u,v). The curl theorem follows from applying Green's theorem in the parameter plane and transforming back. The key identity is that the exterior derivative satisfies d² = 0 (Poincaré lemma), from which Stokes' theorem follows as ∫_{∂M} ω = ∫_M dω for a differential form ω on manifold M.
equations.working_example: F = (−y, x, 0). ∇×F = (0, 0, 2). For the unit circle C in the xy-plane: ∮_C F·dr = ∮ (−y dx + x dy). Parametrize: x = cosθ, y = sinθ: integral = ∫₀^{2π} (sin²θ + cos²θ)dθ = 2π. Surface integral: ∬ 2 dA = 2π(1)² = 2π. Both give 2π.
equations.negation_failure_case: Stokes' theorem requires the surface to be orientable and the field to be smooth. On a Möbius strip (non-orientable surface), the theorem does not apply — there is no consistent choice of normal direction. For fields with singularities (e.g., F = (−y/(x²+y²), x/(x²+y²), 0) with a singularity at the origin), the line integral around the origin gives 2π but the curl is zero everywhere else, demonstrating the importance of the smoothness requirement.
equations.description: The line integral of a vector field around a closed curve equals the surface integral of its curl over any surface bounded by that curve. It generalizes Green's theorem to 3D and unifies all fundamental theorems of vector calculus under the framework of differential forms.

equations.name: Shannon Channel Capacity
equations.domain_of_applicability: The maximum rate at which information can be reliably transmitted over a communication channel with bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N. It sets the absolute physical limit on data rates and drove the design of modern communications from Wi-Fi to 5G.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Shannon showed that for a Gaussian channel, the mutual information I(X;Y) is maximized when the input X is Gaussian. For bandwidth B, the channel carries 2B independent samples per second (Nyquist). Each sample's information capacity is ½ log₂(1 + S/N) bits, giving C = B log₂(1 + S/N). The noisy channel coding theorem proves that rates below C are achievable with arbitrarily low error probability using sufficiently long codes.
equations.working_example: Standard Wi-Fi channel: B = 20 MHz, S/N = 100 (20 dB). C = 20×10⁶ × log₂(101) = 20×10⁶ × 6.66 = 133 Mbps theoretical max. Real Wi-Fi achieves ~65–70% of Shannon capacity due to protocol overhead.
equations.negation_failure_case: Shannon capacity cannot be exceeded by any coding scheme — it is a mathematical upper bound. Attempting to transmit above C inevitably introduces errors. Before Shannon, engineers assumed there was a fundamental tradeoff between rate and error probability; Shannon proved that error-free communication at rates up to C is possible (but not above). Early systems operated far below C; modern LDPC and turbo codes approach within 0.1 dB.
equations.description: The maximum rate at which information can be reliably transmitted over a communication channel with bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N. It sets the absolute physical limit on data rates and drove the design of modern communications from Wi-Fi to 5G.

equations.name: Euler's Buckling Formula
equations.domain_of_applicability: Predicts the critical axial load at which a slender column buckles elastically. Below P_cr, the column compresses uniformly; at P_cr, it suddenly bows sideways.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Consider a pin-ended column of length L with axial load P. The lateral displacement y(x) satisfies the beam equation: EI d²y/dx² = −Py. This is a second-order ODE: y'' + (P/EI)y = 0 with solution y = A sin(√(P/EI) x). Boundary conditions y(0) = y(L) = 0 require √(P/EI) L = nπ. The lowest (n=1) critical load is P_cr = π²EI/L². For other end conditions, the effective length factor K modifies this to P_cr = π²EI/(KL)².
equations.working_example: Steel column (E = 200 GPa), W150×22 section (I = 12.1×10⁻⁶ m⁴), L = 4 m, pin-ended (K = 1). P_cr = π²(200×10⁹)(12.1×10⁻⁶)/(16) = 1,492 kN. For fixed-fixed (K = 0.5): P_cr = 1,492/(0.25) = 5,968 kN — 4× higher.
equations.negation_failure_case: Euler's formula assumes: (1) perfectly straight column, (2) load perfectly axial, (3) elastic material. Failures: (i) Real columns have initial imperfections — even 1/1000 L eccentricity can reduce actual buckling load by 20–40% (Perry–Robertson formula). (ii) For short, stocky columns (slenderness ratio KL/r < ~40 for steel), the material yields before elastic buckling occurs, and the Johnson parabola or Engesser formula must be used instead.
equations.description: Predicts the critical axial load at which a slender column buckles elastically. Below P_cr, the column compresses uniformly; at P_cr, it suddenly bows sideways. It governs the design of structural columns, aircraft fuselage frames, and bridge members.

equations.name: PID Controller
equations.formula: u(t) = K_p e + K_i ∫e dt + K_d de/dt
equations.symbols: u(t) = K_p e + K_i ∫e dt + K_d de/dt
equations.domain_of_applicability: The proportional–integral–derivative controller is the most widely used feedback control law in industry. The proportional term reacts to current error, the integral term eliminates steady-state error, and the derivative term damps oscillations.
key_assumptions: (1) Processes with long dead time — if the delay is comparable to the process time constant, PID oscillates or becomes unstable; Smith predictors or model predictive control (MPC) are needed.
equations.derivation_summary: Derived from control theory requirements: (1) Proportional: output proportional to error e(t) = setpoint − process variable. (2) Integral: accumulated error over time eliminates steady-state offset (since ∫e dt grows until e → 0). (3) Derivative: rate of change of error provides damping (anticipates future error). In the Laplace domain: U(s) = (K_p + K_i/s + K_ds)E(s). The transfer function creates zeros that improve closed-loop stability.
equations.working_example: Temperature control: setpoint 100°C, current 80°C, K_p = 5, K_i = 0.1, K_d = 2. Error e = 20°C, ∫e dt ≈ 200°C·s (accumulated over 10s), de/dt = +2°C/s (temperature rising). u = 5(20) + 0.1(200) + 2(2) = 100 + 20 + 4 = 124 units of heater power.
equations.negation_failure_case: PID fails for: (1) Processes with long dead time — if the delay is comparable to the process time constant, PID oscillates or becomes unstable; Smith predictors or model predictive control (MPC) are needed. (2) Nonlinear processes (pH control, exothermic reactors) where gains vary with operating point. (3) Multivariable (MIMO) systems where coupled variables require matrix-based controllers.
equations.source_citation: Minorsky, J. Am. Soc. Nav. Eng. (1922)
equations.description: The proportional–integral–derivative controller is the most widely used feedback control law in industry. The proportional term reacts to current error, the integral term eliminates steady-state error, and the derivative term damps oscillations. Over 95% of industrial control loops use PID.

equations.name: Beam Bending (Euler–Bernoulli)
equations.domain_of_applicability: Relates the bending moment in a beam to the stress distribution, cross-section geometry, and curvature. It is the most used equation in structural engineering, enabling the design of beams, floors, bridges, and aircraft wings.
key_assumptions: (1) Deep beams (depth/span > 0.
es small-angle assumptions — the exact elastica equation must be solved.
equations.derivation_summary: Assumptions: plane sections remain plane (Bernoulli hypothesis) and material is linearly elastic. A fiber at distance y from the neutral axis has strain ε = y/R (from geometry of bending). Stress: σ = Eε = Ey/R. The internal moment: M = ∫ σ y dA = (E/R)∫ y² dA = EI/R, where I = ∫ y² dA is the second moment of area. Therefore M/I = E/R and σ = My/I.
equations.working_example: Simply supported beam, span 6 m, uniform load 10 kN/m. Max moment: M = wL²/8 = 10(36)/8 = 45 kN·m. Using W200×36 steel section (I = 34.4×10⁻⁶ m⁴, depth 201 mm): max stress σ = My/I = 45000(0.1005)/(34.4×10⁻⁶) = 131 MPa. Yield stress of A36 steel = 250 MPa, so safety factor = 250/131 = 1.91.
equations.negation_failure_case: Euler–Bernoulli fails for: (1) Deep beams (depth/span > 0.2) where shear deformation is significant — Timoshenko beam theory adds shear correction. (2) Composite beams (reinforced concrete, FRP) where E varies across the section. (3) Large deflections where geometric nonlinearity invalidates small-angle assumptions — the exact elastica equation must be solved.
equations.description: Relates the bending moment in a beam to the stress distribution, cross-section geometry, and curvature. It is the most used equation in structural engineering, enabling the design of beams, floors, bridges, and aircraft wings.

equations.name: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
equations.domain_of_applicability: The sum of all voltage drops and rises around any closed loop in a circuit equals zero. This is a consequence of energy conservation (or equivalently, the electrostatic field being conservative) and is one of two fundamental circuit analysis tools.
key_assumptions: (1) Time-varying magnetic flux links the loop — Faraday's law adds an EMF term: ΣV = −dΦ_B/dt.
equations.derivation_summary: For a conservative electric field, ∮ E·dl = 0 around any closed path. In a circuit, this becomes Σ V_k = 0 around any loop. Each element (resistor, source, etc.) contributes a voltage rise or drop. The sum must be zero because a charge returning to its starting point must have the same potential energy.
equations.working_example: Loop with V_source = 12V, R₁ = 4Ω, R₂ = 8Ω in series. KVL: 12 − 4I − 8I = 0. I = 12/12 = 1A. V_R1 = 4V, V_R2 = 8V. Check: 12 − 4 − 8 = 0.
equations.negation_failure_case: KVL breaks down when: (1) Time-varying magnetic flux links the loop — Faraday's law adds an EMF term: ΣV = −dΦ_B/dt. In a transformer, the induced EMF violates naive KVL. (2) At high frequencies (GHz circuits), distributed-element effects mean 'lumped' voltage drops are not well-defined; transmission-line theory replaces KVL. (3) In superconducting loops, flux quantization imposes Φ = nΦ₀, modifying KVL at the quantum level.
equations.description: The sum of all voltage drops and rises around any closed loop in a circuit equals zero. This is a consequence of energy conservation (or equivalently, the electrostatic field being conservative) and is one of two fundamental circuit analysis tools.

equations.name: Nyquist–Shannon Sampling Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: To perfectly reconstruct a bandlimited signal from discrete samples, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency present. This is the theoretical foundation of all digital audio, video, and communication systems.
key_assumptions: Idealized conditions
See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: A bandlimited signal (F(ω) = 0 for |ω| > 2πf_max) sampled at rate f_s produces a spectrum that is periodically replicated at intervals of f_s. If f_s ≥ 2f_max, the copies don't overlap and the original spectrum can be recovered by an ideal low-pass filter. If f_s < 2f_max, the copies overlap (aliasing) and reconstruction is impossible.
equations.working_example: CD audio: f_max = 20 kHz (human hearing limit). Minimum f_s = 40 kHz. CDs use f_s = 44.1 kHz (10% margin). Each sample is 16 bits, giving bit rate = 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bps = 1.41 Mbps for stereo.
