(2) The law deviates at both extremes — the highest-frequency words are somewhat below prediction, and rare words deviate due to sampling limitations. (3) Random concatenation of characters also produces Zipf-like distributions ('monkey typing' argument), so the law alone doesn't prove anything deep about language.
equations.source_citation: Zipf, Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort (1949)
equations.description: In natural language, word frequency is approximately inversely proportional to its rank. The most frequent word occurs roughly twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, etc. This power-law distribution appears in many human-generated data systems.

equations.name: Heaps' Law (Vocabulary Growth)
equations.domain_of_applicability: The number of unique word types V grows sublinearly with the number of tokens n. This means larger corpora continue to produce new words but at a decreasing rate.
key_assumptions: (1) Very small corpora where vocabulary grows nearly linearly.
equations.derivation_summary: If word frequencies follow a Zipf distribution with exponent s, then the expected number of distinct types in a sample of n tokens is V(n) ∝ n^(1/s) (for s > 1). Since s ≈ 1, the exponent β = 1/s ≈ 0.5–1.0, depending on the corpus. Heaps' law can be derived formally from the Zipf distribution using a Poisson sampling model.
equations.working_example: English text: K = 44, β = 0.49. At n = 10,000 tokens: V = 44(10000)^0.49 = 44 × 97.7 = 4,299 unique words. At n = 1,000,000: V = 44(10⁶)^0.49 = 44 × 776 = 34,100 unique words. Doubling the corpus from 500K to 1M tokens adds only ~15% more vocabulary.
equations.negation_failure_case: Heaps' law breaks down for: (1) Very small corpora where vocabulary grows nearly linearly. (2) Technical texts with specialized terminology that is highly repeated (low β). (3) Web-scale corpora where user-generated content (typos, neologisms, code-switching) creates a long tail of hapax legomena that inflates V beyond the smooth power-law prediction.
equations.description: The number of unique word types V grows sublinearly with the number of tokens n. This means larger corpora continue to produce new words but at a decreasing rate. It is mathematically linked to Zipf's law.

equations.name: Median Voter Theorem
equations.domain_of_applicability: Under majority rule with single-peaked preferences on a one-dimensional issue space, the median voter's ideal point is the Condorcet winner — it beats every alternative in pairwise majority voting. This predicts policy convergence toward the center in two-party systems.
key_assumptions: (1) Issues are multidimensional — no stable majority winner may exist (McKelvey's chaos theorem: any outcome can be reached from any other through a sequence of majority votes).
equations.derivation_summary: Consider alternatives on a line with voters having single-peaked preferences. The median voter m's ideal point x_m beats any alternative y: if y < x_m, all voters with ideal points ≥ x_m (a majority, since x_m is the median) prefer x_m. If y > x_m, all voters with ideal points ≤ x_m prefer x_m. Therefore x_m wins every pairwise contest.
equations.working_example: 11 voters with ideal points {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}. Median = 5. Test: 5 vs 7: voters at {1,2,3,4,5,5,6} prefer 5 (7 votes vs 4). 5 vs 3: voters at {4,5,5,6,7,8,9,10} prefer 5 (8 votes vs 3). The median always wins.
equations.negation_failure_case: The theorem fails when: (1) Issues are multidimensional — no stable majority winner may exist (McKelvey's chaos theorem: any outcome can be reached from any other through a sequence of majority votes). (2) Preferences are not single-peaked (e.g., extremists prefer either extreme to the center). (3) Voters are strategic (not sincere) — agenda control and vote trading can override the median. (4) Voter turnout is unequal, so the decisive voter is not the population median.
equations.description: Under majority rule with single-peaked preferences on a one-dimensional issue space, the median voter's ideal point is the Condorcet winner — it beats every alternative in pairwise majority voting. This predicts policy convergence toward the center in two-party systems.

equations.name: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
equations.formula: No SWF satisfies U, P, I, and D simultaneously
equations.symbols: No SWF satisfies U, P, I, and D simultaneously
equations.domain_of_applicability: No social welfare function (aggregating individual preferences into a social ranking) can simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain (U), Pareto efficiency (P), independence of irrelevant alternatives (I), and non-dictatorship (D). This foundational negative result constrains all voting system design.
key_assumptions: See negation section for detailed failure modes
equations.derivation_summary: Arrow proved this by contradiction. Assume a SWF satisfies U, P, and I. Show that there must exist a 'decisive' set for every pair of alternatives. Show that decisive sets must be nested (intersection is also decisive). By a sequence of contractions, show the intersection reduces to a single individual — a dictator — violating D.
equations.working_example: Consider 3 voters ranking {A, B, C}. Voter 1: A>B>C. Voter 2: B>C>A. Voter 3: C>A>B. Majority rule: A beats B (2:1), B beats C (2:1), but C beats A (2:1) — a Condorcet cycle with no consistent social ranking. Any attempt to resolve this must violate at least one of Arrow's conditions.
equations.negation_failure_case: The impossibility is not absolute — relaxing any axiom yields possibility: (1) Restricting the domain to single-peaked preferences (median voter works). (2) Allowing cardinal utilities (scored voting, approval voting) bypasses the ordinal framework. (3) Accepting probabilistic or partial orderings. (4) Sen's liberal paradox shows additional impossibilities even with weaker conditions. The theorem constrains but doesn't eliminate institutional design.
equations.source_citation: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951)
equations.description: No social welfare function (aggregating individual preferences into a social ranking) can simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain (U), Pareto efficiency (P), independence of irrelevant alternatives (I), and non-dictatorship (D). This foundational negative result constrains all voting system design.
